context: A triangle with an area of 6 square units is transformed by multiplying each vertex’s column matrix on the left by [[2, 1], [0, 3]]. What is the area of the new triangle?

why.A: Correct — a linear transformation multiplies every area by the absolute value of its determinant, 2 × 3 − 1 × 0 = 6.
why.B: This multiplies by the trace, 2 + 3. Areas scale by the determinant.
why.C: This adds the determinant to the area instead of multiplying.
why.D: This multiplies by the square of the determinant, as if each length scaled by 6.

context: Matrices A and B are 2 × 2, det A = 3 and det B = −2. What is det(A⁻¹B)?

why.A: This uses det A instead of det(A⁻¹). The inverse has the reciprocal determinant.
why.B: Correct — det(A⁻¹B) = det(A⁻¹) · det B = (1/3)(−2).
why.C: This multiplies the determinants and also drops the negative sign.
why.D: This divides det A by det B, the ratio upside down.

context: For what positive value of k is the determinant of [[k, 2], [4, k]] equal to the sum of its diagonal entries?

why.A: This sets the determinant equal to 0 instead of to the diagonal sum.
why.B: This drops the −8 from the determinant, solving k² = 2k.
why.C: Correct — k² − 8 = 2k gives k² − 2k − 8 = (k − 4)(k + 2) = 0, and the positive root is 4.
why.D: This multiplies the off-diagonal entries to 4 instead of 8, solving k² − 4 = 2k.

context: Let A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] and B = [[1, 0], [3, 1]]. What is the top-left entry of AB − BA?

why.A: This assumes AB = BA. Matrix multiplication usually depends on order.
why.B: This is the top-left entry of AB alone.
why.C: This computes BA − AB, the difference in the opposite order.
why.D: Correct — AB = [[7, 2], [3, 1]] and BA = [[1, 2], [3, 7]], so the top-left entry of AB − BA is 7 − 1.

context: In the complex plane, the horizontal axis shows the real part and the vertical axis shows the imaginary part. What point represents −3 + 2i?

why.A: Correct — the real part, −3, is the horizontal coordinate, and the imaginary part, 2, is the vertical one.
why.B: This swaps the axes, putting the imaginary part first.
why.C: This negates both parts, which gives the point for 3 − 2i.
why.D: This is the point for the conjugate, −3 − 2i.

context: What is (−i)²?

why.A: This squares away the minus sign but forgets that i² = −1.
why.C: This doubles −i instead of squaring it.
why.D: This treats squaring as simply removing the minus sign.

context: In the complex plane, what number is the midpoint of the segment joining 2 + 5i and 6 − i?

why.A: This is the sum of the two numbers. The midpoint is half the sum.
why.B: This is half the difference, (6 − i − (2 + 5i))/2, which is half the vector from one point to the other.
why.C: Correct — average the parts: (2 + 6)/2 = 4 and (5 + (−1))/2 = 2.
why.D: This averages the imaginary parts as (5 + 1)/2, dropping the sign of −i.

context: In the complex plane, what is the distance between 2 − i and −4 + 7i?

why.A: This adds the horizontal and vertical gaps, 6 + 8. The distance is along the diagonal.
why.B: This is the square of the distance, before the square root.
why.C: This adds the two numbers, −2 + 6i, and finds its absolute value. Distance uses the difference.
why.D: Correct — the difference is −6 + 8i, and its absolute value is √((−6)² + 8²) = √100 = 10.

context: Multiplying 4 + 3i by i moves its point in the complex plane. At what point does i(4 + 3i) lie?

why.A: Correct — i(4 + 3i) = 4i + 3i² = −3 + 4i, which is the point turned 90° counterclockwise.
why.B: This multiplies by −i, which turns the point clockwise.
why.C: This swaps the parts but forgets that i² = −1.
why.D: This multiplies by −1, which turns the point 180°.

context: If 2z + i = 4 − 3i, what is z?

why.A: This divides 4 − 3i by 2 before subtracting i, and never moves the i.
why.B: Correct — subtracting i gives 2z = 4 − 4i, and dividing by 2 gives z = 2 − 2i.
why.C: This subtracts i but forgets to divide by 2.
why.D: This adds i instead of subtracting it, giving 2z = 4 − 2i.

context: For real numbers a and b, what is the sum of a + bi and its complex conjugate?

why.A: This is the difference, (a + bi) − (a − bi), not the sum.
why.B: This is the product of the number and its conjugate, not the sum.
why.C: Correct — (a + bi) + (a − bi) = 2a. The imaginary parts cancel.
why.D: This assumes both parts cancel. Only the imaginary parts have opposite signs.

context: A complex number z has |z| = 5, the sum of z and its conjugate is 6, and the imaginary part of z is positive. What is z?

why.A: This has the right size and real part, but its imaginary part is negative.
why.B: This swaps the real and imaginary parts. Its conjugate sum is 8.
why.C: This uses the modulus, 5, as the imaginary part. That number has an absolute value of √34.
why.D: Correct — z plus its conjugate is twice the real part, so the real part is 3. Then 3² + b² = 25 gives b = 4, taking the positive value.

context: For which of the following values of n does iⁿ + iⁿ⁺¹ = 1 − i?

why.A: Correct — 11 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, so i¹¹ = −i and i¹² = 1, which add to 1 − i.
why.B: Here i¹² = 1 and i¹³ = i, which add to 1 + i.
why.C: Here i¹³ = i and i¹⁴ = −1, which add to −1 + i.
why.D: Here i¹⁴ = −1 and i¹⁵ = −i, which add to −1 − i.

context: For what positive real value of k is (1 + ki)² a purely imaginary number?

why.A: This makes the square a real number, 1, instead of a purely imaginary one.
why.B: Correct — (1 + ki)² = (1 − k²) + 2ki, which is purely imaginary when 1 − k² = 0, and the positive root is k = 1.
why.C: This sets the imaginary part 2k equal to 1. The condition is on the real part.
why.D: This also makes the real part 0, but it is not positive.

context: The complex number z = 2(cos 60° + i sin 60°) has absolute value 2 and angle 60°. What is z³?

why.A: This triples the angle to 180° but reads cos 180° as 1 instead of −1.
why.B: This multiplies the absolute value by 3 instead of cubing it.
why.C: Correct — cubing cubes the absolute value, 2³ = 8, and triples the angle to 180°, which points along the negative real axis.
why.D: This treats 180° as pointing up the imaginary axis. That direction is 90°.

context: The temperature at dawn was −8°F. By noon it had risen 15°F. What was the temperature at noon, in degrees Fahrenheit?

why.A: This subtracts the 15-degree rise instead of adding it.
why.B: Correct — rising 15 degrees from −8 gives −8 + 15 = 7.
why.C: This adds 8 and 15 and ignores that the dawn reading was below zero.
why.D: This finds the 7-degree gap but keeps the negative sign from the dawn reading.

context: Which of the following is NOT a factor of 84?

why.A: This is a factor: 84 = 12 × 7.
why.B: This is a factor: 84 = 14 × 6.
why.C: Correct — 84 ÷ 16 = 5.25, which is not a whole number, so 16 is not a factor.
why.D: This is a factor: 84 = 21 × 4.

context: How many integers lie between −3.2 and 4.6 on the number line?

why.A: This subtracts 4 − (−3) = 7, which counts the gaps between the integers rather than the integers themselves.
why.B: This rounds 4.6 up to 5 and counts it, but 5 lies beyond 4.6.
why.C: This drops the negative sign and counts only 3 and 4, the integers between 3.2 and 4.6.
why.D: Correct — the integers are −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

context: A parking garage charges $3 for the first hour and $2 for each additional hour or part of an hour. How much does it cost to park for 4 hours 20 minutes?

why.A: Correct — after the first hour, 3 hours 20 minutes remain, which is 4 charged hours: $3 + 4 × $2 = $11.
why.B: This charges only 3 additional hours and ignores the 20 minutes. Any part of an hour is charged as a full hour.
why.C: This charges $2 for 5 additional hours, counting the first hour again.
why.D: This charges $2 for each of 5 hours and ignores the $3 first-hour rate.

context: What is the product of all the integers from −4 to 5, inclusive?

why.A: This multiplies (−4)(−3)(−2)(−1) = 24 by 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 = 120 and skips 0.
why.B: Correct — 0 is one of the integers from −4 to 5, so the whole product is 0.
why.C: This skips 0 and also treats the product of four negative numbers as negative.
why.D: This multiplies only the positive integers, 1 through 5.

context: How many integers from 1 to 60 are multiples of 4 but not multiples of 6?

why.A: This counts every multiple of 4 and removes none of the multiples of 6.
why.B: This counts the multiples of 12, the numbers to be removed, not the ones left.
why.C: Correct — there are 15 multiples of 4, and 5 of them (12, 24, 36, 48, 60) are also multiples of 6, leaving 10.
why.D: This counts the numbers that are multiples of 4 or of 6, 15 + 10 − 5.

context: If −3 ≤ a ≤ 2 and −1 ≤ b ≤ 4, what is the greatest possible value of a − b?

why.A: This takes the greatest value of each, 2 − 4. Subtracting a large b makes the difference smaller.
why.B: This adds the two greatest values, 2 + 4, instead of subtracting.
why.C: This is the least possible value of a − b, −3 − 4.
why.D: Correct — a − b is greatest when a is as large as possible and b as small as possible: 2 − (−1) = 3.

context: How many integers x satisfy x² < 30?

why.A: Correct — x² < 30 holds for −5 ≤ x ≤ 5, since 5² = 25 and 6² = 36. That is 5 negative integers, 0 and 5 positive integers.
why.B: This counts only the positive integers 1 through 5. Negative integers have positive squares too.
why.C: This counts 1 through 5 and −1 through −5 but leaves out 0, whose square is 0.
why.D: This counts 0 through 5 and misses the negative integers.

context: The decimal form of 3/7 is 0.428571428571…, in which the six digits 428571 repeat forever. What is the 50th digit after the decimal point?

why.A: This is the 48th digit, the end of the eighth full block. The 2 leftover digits still have to be counted.
why.B: Correct — 50 = 6 × 8 + 2, so 8 full blocks use 48 digits and the 50th digit is the 2nd digit of the block, 2.
why.C: This is the 49th digit, counting only the first of the 2 leftover digits.
why.D: This is the 51st digit, counting one digit too many into the ninth block.

context: How many positive integers less than 50 have exactly 3 positive divisors?

why.A: This counts every perfect square from 1 to 49. 1 has one divisor, and 16 and 36 have more than three.
why.B: This counts the perfect squares from 4 to 49. 16 has 5 divisors and 36 has 9, so not every square qualifies.
why.C: Correct — only the square of a prime has exactly 3 divisors (1, p and p²). Those less than 50 are 4, 9, 25 and 49.
why.D: This counts the primes less than 50, which have exactly 2 divisors.

context: How many of the positive divisors of 720 = 2⁴ · 3² · 5 are perfect squares?

why.A: This counts all the divisors of 720, (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1), not just the square ones.
why.B: This finds the square divisors but leaves out 1, which is a perfect square.
why.C: This counts only the choices for the power of 2 and forgets to combine them with the powers of 3.
why.D: Correct — a square divisor uses even exponents only: 2⁰, 2² or 2⁴ (3 ways), 3⁰ or 3² (2 ways) and 5⁰ (1 way). That gives 3 × 2 × 1 = 6: 1, 4, 16, 9, 36 and 144.

context: A square has an area of 45 square inches. What is its side length, in inches, in simplest radical form?

why.A: Correct — the side is √45 = √(9 · 5) = 3√5.
why.B: This swaps the roles of the factors. 5√3 is √75; the perfect square inside 45 is 9, not 25.
why.C: This halves the area instead of taking its square root.
why.D: This pulls out the factor 9 without taking its square root.

context: What is the value of (2/5)⁻²?

why.A: This squares 2/5 and ignores the negative sign on the exponent.
why.B: Correct — a negative exponent flips the fraction: (2/5)⁻² = (5/2)² = 25/4.
why.C: This treats the negative exponent as making the result negative. It flips the fraction instead.
why.D: This flips the fraction but forgets to square it.

context: What is the value of 9^(1/2) + 8^(1/3)?

why.A: This multiplies each base by its exponent, 9 × 1/2 + 8 × 1/3. A fractional exponent is a root.
why.B: This takes √9 = 3 but halves 8 instead of taking its cube root.
why.C: Correct — 9^(1/2) = √9 = 3 and 8^(1/3) = ∛8 = 2, so the sum is 5.
why.D: This adds the bases first, then takes a square root. Each term has to be evaluated separately.

context: The mass of Earth is about 6.0 × 10²⁴ kilograms, and the mass of the Moon is about 7.0 × 10²² kilograms. Earth’s mass is about how many times the Moon’s mass?

why.A: This subtracts the exponents but uses 10¹ instead of 10².
why.B: This uses 10³ for the power of ten instead of 10²⁴⁻²² = 10².
why.C: This divides the Moon’s mass by Earth’s, the ratio upside down.

context: What is the solution to √(x − 4) + 3 = 8?

why.A: Correct — subtract 3 to get √(x − 4) = 5, square to get x − 4 = 25, and x = 29.
why.B: This isolates the root but never squares: x − 4 = 5.
why.C: This squares each term before isolating the root, getting (x − 4) + 9 = 64.
why.D: This squares correctly to get 25 but then subtracts 4 instead of adding it.

context: The population of a town t years from now is modeled by P = 2,000(1.05)ᵗ. What does the 1.05 tell you about the population?

choices.text: It grows by 1.05 people each year.
It grows by 5 people each year.

why.A: This reads the whole multiplier as the growth. Growing by 105% would more than double the population.
why.B: Correct — each year the population is multiplied by 1.05, which is 100% of itself plus 5%.
why.C: This reads the multiplier as a fixed number added each year, as in a linear model.
why.D: This reads the 5 in 1.05 as a count. The growth is a percent of the current population.

context: If √a = 3√2 and √b = 2√3, what is √(ab)?

why.A: This multiplies the coefficients but adds the numbers under the radicals.
why.B: This adds the coefficients and adds the numbers under the radicals.
why.D: This finds ab = 18 × 12 = 216 and forgets to take the square root.

context: What is the value of √(x¹⁰) when x = −2?

why.A: This simplifies √(x¹⁰) to x⁵ and substitutes. For negative x, √(x¹⁰) equals −x⁵, not x⁵.
why.B: This evaluates (−2)¹⁰ and forgets to take the square root.
why.C: This multiplies −2 by 5, treating the exponent as a factor.
why.D: Correct — (−2)¹⁰ = 1,024, and √1,024 = 32. A square root is never negative.

context: Which of the following numbers is greatest?

why.A: Correct — 3²⁰ = (3²)¹⁰ = 9¹⁰ and 2³⁰ = (2³)¹⁰ = 8¹⁰, so 3²⁰ is larger than 2³⁰. It is about 3.5 × 10⁹, beating 5¹² ≈ 2.4 × 10⁸ and 10⁸.
why.B: This picks the largest exponent. 2³⁰ = 8¹⁰, which is less than 9¹⁰ = 3²⁰.
why.C: This picks the largest base. 10⁸ is only 100 million.
why.D: This is about 2.4 × 10⁸, far below 3²⁰.

context: If x = 2ᵏ and y = 2ᵏ⁺³, which expression gives y in terms of x?

why.A: This adds 3 to x. Adding 3 to the exponent multiplies the power by 2³.
why.B: Correct — 2ᵏ⁺³ = 2ᵏ · 2³ = 8 · 2ᵏ = 8x.
why.C: This cubes x, as if the exponent were multiplied by 3 instead of increased by 3.
why.D: This multiplies x by the 3 from the exponent rather than by 2³.

context: A car loses 20% of its value each year. After how many whole years will it first be worth less than half of its original value?

why.A: This takes 20% of the original price each year, so 3 years would cost 60%. Each year’s loss is 20% of a smaller value, and 0.8³ = 0.512.
why.B: This divides 50% by 20%, as if the car lost the same dollar amount every year.
why.C: Correct — the value is multiplied by 0.8 each year: 0.8³ = 0.512 is still above half, and 0.8⁴ ≈ 0.41 is the first below it.
why.D: This uses 0.2 as the yearly multiplier. 0.2 is the fraction lost; the fraction kept is 0.8.

context: For a group of students, the line of best fit relating hours studied, h, to predicted test score, s, is s = 4.5h + 62. According to the model, by how many points does the predicted score increase for each additional hour of study?

why.A: This is the intercept, the predicted score for a student who studies 0 hours.
why.B: This is the predicted score after 1 hour, 4.5 + 62, not the change per hour.
why.C: This is 1 ÷ 4.5, the hours per point, the rate turned upside down.
why.D: Correct — the slope, 4.5, is the change in the predicted score for each 1-hour increase in h.

context: A histogram shows the test scores of 25 students: 4 scored from 60 to 69, 9 from 70 to 79, 7 from 80 to 89, and 5 from 90 to 99. How many students scored 80 or higher?

why.A: Correct — the 80–89 and 90–99 bars together hold 7 + 5 = 12 students.
why.B: This reads only the 80–89 bar and leaves out the 90–99 bar.
why.C: This reads only the 90–99 bar.
why.D: This also counts the 70–79 bar, whose scores are all below 80.

context: In a random sample of 200 of a city’s 50,000 voters, 116 said they support building a new park. Based on the sample, about how many of the city’s voters support the park?

why.A: This is the count within the sample. The question asks about all 50,000 voters.
why.B: Correct — 116/200 = 58% of the sample, and 58% of 50,000 is 29,000.
why.C: This is the 42% of voters the sample suggests do not support the park.
why.D: This scales the sample up by 100. The city is 250 times the size of the sample.

context: The line of best fit for a data set is y = 2x + 5. One data point is (6, 20). What is the residual for this point, the actual y-value minus the predicted y-value?

why.A: This subtracts in the wrong order, predicted minus actual.
why.B: This is the predicted y-value, not the residual.
why.C: Correct — the line predicts 2(6) + 5 = 17, and 20 − 17 = 3.
why.D: This subtracts the x-value 6 from the y-value 20 and never uses the line.

context: A histogram shows the wait times of 20 customers: 7 waited 0–9 minutes, 4 waited 10–19 minutes, 6 waited 20–29 minutes, and 3 waited 30–39 minutes. Which interval contains the median wait time?

why.A: This is the tallest bar, which holds the mode, not the median.
why.B: This picks the interval just past the middle of the axis. The median depends on where the 10th and 11th customers fall, not on the axis.
why.C: The individual times are unknown, but the counts are enough to locate the 10th and 11th values within one interval.
why.D: Correct — the median lies between the 10th and 11th wait times. The first bar holds the 1st through 7th, and the second holds the 8th through 11th.

context: A line of best fit models the monthly rent p, in dollars, of apartments in a city as p = 1.2s + 300, where s is the floor area in square feet. What does the 1.2 represent?

choices.text: Each added square foot raises the predicted rent by $1.20.
Every apartment rents for exactly $1.20 per square foot.
A 1-square-foot apartment is predicted to rent for $1.20.
Each added dollar of rent adds 1.2 square feet of area.

why.A: Correct — 1.2 is the slope: the change in predicted rent, in dollars, per square foot of area.
why.B: This ignores the $300 and treats a model of a trend as an exact price for every apartment.
why.C: At s = 1 the model predicts 1.2 + 300 = $301.20.
why.D: This reverses the roles of the variables. The model predicts rent from area.

context: A principal wants to estimate the average number of hours per week that the school’s 1,200 students spend on homework. Which sample is most likely to represent all the students?

choices.text: the first 50 students to arrive one morning
50 students picked at random from the school roster
50 students in the honors study hall
50 students who answer a survey link online

why.A: Early arrivals share schedules and habits, such as a bus route or a morning activity, so they may differ from the rest.
why.B: Correct — random selection from the whole roster gives every student the same chance of being chosen.
why.C: Honors students likely do more homework than average, so this sample would run high.
why.D: Volunteers choose themselves, and students with strong feelings about homework are more likely to answer.

context: A survey asked 120 people which of two parks they prefer. Of the 70 adults, 45 prefer North Park. Of the 50 teenagers, 30 prefer North Park. What percent of the people who prefer North Park are teenagers?

why.A: This is the percent of teenagers who prefer North Park, 30/50. The question divides by the people who prefer North Park.
why.B: This divides the 30 teenagers by all 120 people surveyed.
why.C: Correct — 45 + 30 = 75 people prefer North Park, and 30 of them are teenagers: 30/75 = 40%.
why.D: This is the percent of everyone surveyed who prefers North Park, 75/120.

context: Which of the following data sets has the smallest standard deviation?

why.A: This set has the smallest values, but they are 2 apart, twice the spacing of 50, 51, 52, 53.
why.B: Every value is 5 away from the mean of 5, so the standard deviation is 5.
why.C: These values are 10 apart, the widest spread of the four.
why.D: Correct — its values sit 1 apart, the tightest spacing of the four sets. Standard deviation measures spread, not the size of the values.

context: The data set 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 95 contains one outlier, 95. When 95 is removed, which of the following decreases by the greatest amount?

why.A: Correct — the range falls from 95 − 12 = 83 to 20 − 12 = 8, a drop of 75. The mean falls only from about 29.2 to 16.
why.B: The mean is pulled by outliers, but it falls only from about 29.2 to 16, about 13. The range depends on the outlier directly.
why.C: The median moves only from 16.5 to 15.
why.D: The mode is 15 both before and after, so it does not change.

context: A set of 6 numbers has a mean of 10. The numbers 4 and 22 are then added to the set. What is the mean of the 8 numbers?

why.A: This averages the old mean, 10, with the mean of the new numbers, 13, as if both groups had the same size.
why.B: Correct — the original sum is 6 × 10 = 60, the new sum is 60 + 26 = 86, and 86 ÷ 8 = 10.75.
why.C: This is the mean of the two added numbers alone.
why.D: This finds the new sum, 86, but divides by the original 6 numbers instead of 8.

context: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 32 and a base of length 10. What is the length of each of the two equal sides?

why.A: This is the two equal sides together. It still has to be split between them.
why.B: This halves the whole perimeter and ignores the base.
why.C: Correct — the two equal sides share 32 − 10 = 22, so each is 11.
why.D: This divides the perimeter by 3, as if the triangle were equilateral.

context: Which of the following sets of side lengths forms a right triangle?

why.A: These start like the 6-8-10 triple, but 36 + 64 = 100, not 144.
why.B: These start like the 5-12-13 triple, but 25 + 144 = 169, not 196.
why.C: 81 + 144 = 225, which would need a longest side of 15, not 16.

context: A triangle has sides of length 4, 6 and 8. A similar triangle has a shortest side of length 10. What is the length of the longest side of the similar triangle?

why.A: Correct — the scale factor is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, and 8 × 2.5 = 20.
why.B: This adds 6 to every side, since 10 − 4 = 6. Similar figures scale by multiplying.
why.C: This doubles the longest side. The scale factor is 2.5, not 2.
why.D: This scales the middle side, 6, instead of the longest side, 8.

context: A right triangle has legs of length 6 and 8. A square is drawn outward on its hypotenuse, so the square and the triangle share that side. What is the total area of the figure formed by the triangle and the square?

why.A: This is the area of the square alone.
why.B: Correct — the hypotenuse is √(36 + 64) = 10, so the square has area 100 and the triangle has area ½ · 6 · 8 = 24.
why.C: This takes the triangle’s area as 6 × 8 = 48, forgetting the ½.
why.D: This uses 6 + 8 = 14 as the hypotenuse, giving a square of 196.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = 8, AC = 10 and angle A measures 30°. What is the area of triangle ABC?

why.A: This multiplies 8 by the height of 5 and forgets the ½.
why.B: This uses sin 60° = √3/2 in place of sin 30° = 1/2.
why.C: Correct — the height from C to line AB is 10 sin 30° = 5, so the area is ½ · 8 · 5 = 20.
why.D: This multiplies the two sides and ignores both the angle and the ½.

context: In triangle ABC, M is the midpoint of AB and N is the midpoint of AC. If MN = 3x − 1 and BC = 4x + 8, what is the length of BC?

why.A: This is the length of MN, half of BC.
why.B: This is the value of x, not the length of BC.
why.C: This doubles BC instead of doubling MN, reversing which segment is half the other.
why.D: Correct — a midsegment is half the third side, so 2(3x − 1) = 4x + 8 gives x = 5 and BC = 28.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = BC = 7 and angle B measures 60°. What is the length of AC?

why.A: Correct — the base angles are equal and share 180° − 60° = 120°, so each is 60° and the triangle is equilateral.
why.B: This uses the ratio for the longer leg of a 30°-60°-90° triangle. The triangle here has three 60° angles.
why.C: This treats the 60° angle as if it were 90° and finds the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle.
why.D: This adds the two given sides, as if AC stretched straight across both of them.

context: How many different integer lengths are possible for the third side of a triangle whose other two sides have lengths 5 and 9?

why.A: This includes 4 and 14. With those lengths the three sides lie flat and do not form a triangle.
why.B: Correct — the third side must be greater than 9 − 5 = 4 and less than 9 + 5 = 14, so it can be 5 through 13, which is 9 lengths.
why.C: This applies only the upper limit, counting 1 through 13.
why.D: This counts only the lengths from 5 to 9, between the two given sides.

context: A student 5 feet tall stands 12 feet from the base of a lamppost. Her shadow, cast by the lamp, is 8 feet long and ends at the tip of the lamppost’s shadow. How tall is the lamppost, in feet?

why.A: This uses the 12-foot distance to the lamppost as its base. The lamppost’s triangle runs all the way to the tip of the shadow, 20 feet.
why.B: This inverts the ratio, setting h/20 = 8/5.
why.C: Correct — the light makes two similar right triangles sharing the shadow’s tip. The lamppost is 12 + 8 = 20 feet from the tip, so h/20 = 5/8 and h = 12.5.
why.D: This adds the 12-foot distance to the student’s height.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = 13, AC = 15 and BC = 14. Point D lies on BC so that AD is perpendicular to BC. What is the length of AD?

why.A: This assumes D is the midpoint of BC, so BD = 7 and AD = √(169 − 49). The foot of an altitude is the midpoint only when AB = AC.
why.B: This also puts D at the midpoint but uses side AC: √(225 − 49). The two sides give different answers, which shows D is not the midpoint.
why.C: This takes the altitude to be the length of the side it is drawn to.
why.D: Correct — let BD = x. Then 13² − x² = 15² − (14 − x)², which gives x = 5, and AD = √(169 − 25) = 12.

context: A hiker walks 5 kilometers north, then 8 kilometers east, then 1 kilometer south. What is the straight-line distance, in kilometers, from her starting point?

why.A: Correct — she ends 5 − 1 = 4 km north and 8 km east of the start, so the distance is √(16 + 64) = √80 = 4√5.
why.B: This uses the first two legs, 5 and 8, and ignores the 1 km walked back south.
why.C: This adds all three distances walked. The straight-line distance is shorter than the path.
why.D: This adds the net north and east distances, 4 + 8, instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.

context: A line on a graph shows the amount of water, in gallons, left in a tank t minutes after a drain is opened. The line passes through (0, 40) and (5, 0). At what rate, in gallons per minute, does the water drain?

why.A: This is the starting amount of water, the line’s y-intercept, not the rate.
why.B: Correct — the water falls 40 gallons in 5 minutes, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8 gallons per minute.
why.C: This is the time the tank takes to empty, the line’s t-intercept.
why.D: This divides 5 by 40, giving minutes per gallon instead of gallons per minute.

context: Which of the following points lies in the region y > 2x + 1?

why.A: This point lies on the line itself, since 2(1) + 1 = 3. The inequality is strict, so the line is not included.
why.B: At x = 2 the boundary is at 5, and 4 is below it.
why.C: Correct — at x = 0 the boundary is at 1, and 3 > 1.
why.D: At x = −1 the boundary is at −1, and −2 is below it.

context: What is the y-intercept of the line 5x − 2y = 20?

why.A: This is the x-intercept, found by setting y = 0.
why.B: This divides 20 by 2 and drops the negative sign on −2y.
why.C: This is the slope computed as −A/B with the sign of −2 dropped. The slope is 5/2, and the question asks for the y-intercept anyway.
why.D: Correct — set x = 0: −2y = 20, so y = −10.

context: On a graph of taxi fares, the fare in dollars is a linear function of the miles driven, and the line passes through (2, 9) and (6, 17). What is the fare, in dollars, for a ride of 0 miles, the flat fee charged at the start of every ride?

why.A: Correct — the slope is (17 − 9)/(6 − 2) = 2 dollars per mile, so the fare at 0 miles is 9 − 2(2) = 5.
why.B: This is the slope, the charge per mile, not the flat fee.
why.C: This is the fare for a 2-mile ride.
why.D: This divides 9 dollars by 2 miles, assuming the whole fare is charged by the mile with no flat fee.

context: What is the shortest distance from the point (5, 2) to the line x = −1?

why.A: This subtracts 1 from 5 instead of subtracting −1.
why.B: Correct — x = −1 is a vertical line, so the shortest path is horizontal: 5 − (−1) = 6.
why.C: This measures to the point (−1, 0). The closest point on the line is (−1, 2), straight across.
why.D: This is the point’s distance to the x-axis, its y-coordinate.

context: A line has an x-intercept of 6 and a y-intercept of −4. What is the slope of the line?

why.A: This divides the y-intercept by the x-intercept, −4/6. The slope is the change in y over the change in x between the two points.
why.B: This divides the change in x by the change in y.
why.C: Correct — the line passes through (0, −4) and (6, 0), so the slope is (0 − (−4))/(6 − 0) = 4/6 = 2/3.
why.D: This divides the x-intercept by the y-intercept, flipping the ratio and the sign.

context: Point A(3, −1) is reflected across the y-axis, and the image is then moved 4 units up. What are the coordinates of the final point?

why.A: This reflects across the x-axis, giving (3, 1), before moving up.
why.B: This reflects correctly but moves 4 units right instead of up.
why.C: This reflects correctly but moves 4 units down instead of up.
why.D: Correct — reflecting across the y-axis negates x, giving (−3, −1), and moving up 4 gives (−3, 3).

context: What is the area of the region in the standard (x, y) coordinate plane where both y ≥ |x| and y ≤ 5?

why.A: Correct — the region is a triangle with vertices (0, 0), (−5, 5) and (5, 5). Its base is 10 and its height is 5, so the area is ½ · 10 · 5 = 25.
why.B: This uses only the half of the region where x ≥ 0. The graph of y = |x| rises on both sides of the y-axis.
why.C: This multiplies the base and height and forgets the ½.
why.D: This treats the region as a 10-by-10 square.

context: Which point is the same distance from each of the points (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 8)?

why.A: This averages the three vertices, which gives the centroid. The centroid is the balance point, not the point equidistant from the vertices.
why.B: Correct — being equidistant from (0, 0) and (6, 0) forces x = 3, and from (0, 0) and (0, 8) forces y = 4. The point is 5 from all three.
why.C: This is equidistant from (0, 0) and (6, 0) only. Its distance to (0, 8) is √73.
why.D: This swaps the coordinates of the correct point.

context: The lines 2x + ky = 6 and 4x − 3y = 1 are parallel. What is the value of k?

why.A: This finds the right size but loses the sign of the slope −2/k.
why.B: This makes the slopes negative reciprocals, which is the condition for perpendicular lines.
why.C: Correct — the second line has slope 4/3, and the first has slope −2/k. Setting −2/k = 4/3 gives k = −3/2.
why.D: This copies the y-coefficient of the second equation, ignoring that its x-coefficient is twice as large.

context: The points (1, 1) and (4, 5) are adjacent vertices of a square. What is the area of the square?

why.A: This treats the two points as opposite corners of a rectangle with sides 3 and 4.
why.B: This is the side length, not the area.
why.C: This treats the segment as a diagonal of the square, giving 5²/2. The points are adjacent, so the segment is a side.
why.D: Correct — the side is the distance between the points, √(3² + 4²) = 5, and the area is 5² = 25.

context: A class has 35 juniors and 25 seniors. Of the juniors, 22 own a bike, and of the seniors, 10 own a bike. One student is chosen at random from the class. What is the probability that the student is a senior who owns a bike?

why.A: Correct — 10 of the 60 students are seniors who own a bike.
why.B: This divides by the 25 seniors instead of all 60 students. The student is chosen from the whole class.
why.C: This divides by the 32 bike owners instead of all 60 students.
why.D: This is the probability that the student owns a bike, 32/60, junior or senior.

context: A spinner is divided into three sectors with central angles of 60°, 120° and 180°. What is the probability that a spin lands in the largest sector?

why.A: This treats the three sectors as equally likely. The probability depends on each sector’s angle.
why.B: Correct — the largest sector takes 180° of the 360° circle.
why.C: This is the probability for the smallest sector, 60/360.
why.D: This is the probability of not landing in the smallest sector.

context: A spinner with red, blue and green sections is spun 50 times. It lands on red 12 times, blue 18 times and green 20 times. Based on these results, what is the experimental probability that a spin does not land on blue?

why.A: This is the probability of landing on blue, 18/50.
why.B: This counts colors, 2 of 3, and ignores the results of the 50 spins.
why.C: Correct — 12 + 20 = 32 of the 50 spins were not blue, and 32/50 = 16/25.
why.D: This compares the 32 non-blue spins with the 18 blue spins. A probability divides by all 50 spins.

context: One card is drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck, which has 26 red cards and 4 kings, 2 of them red. What is the probability that the card is red or a king?

why.A: This adds 26 and 4 and counts the 2 red kings twice.
why.B: This is the probability of a red king, a card that is red and a king.
why.C: This counts only the red cards and leaves out the black kings.
why.D: Correct — 26 red cards plus the 2 black kings make 28 cards, and 28/52 = 7/13.

context: A pizza shop offers 8 toppings. How many different pizzas with exactly 2 different toppings are possible?

why.A: Correct — the order of the toppings does not matter, so the count is (8 × 7) ÷ 2 = 28.
why.B: This counts ordered pairs, 8 × 7. Mushroom-and-onion is the same pizza as onion-and-mushroom.
why.C: This allows the same topping twice and counts order, 8 × 8.
why.D: This multiplies the number of toppings by the number chosen, 8 × 2.

context: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even?

why.A: This assumes even and odd products are equally likely. One even factor is enough to make the product even.
why.B: Correct — the product is odd only when both dice are odd, with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, so it is even with probability 3/4.
why.C: This is the probability that the product is odd.
why.D: This adds the chances that each die is even, 1/2 + 1/2, counting the rolls where both are even twice.

context: At a school, 40% of the students are in the band, and 30% of the band members are also in the choir. What percent of all the students are in both the band and the choir?

why.A: This adds the two percents. The 30% is a share of the band, not of the school.
why.B: This subtracts the two percents.
why.C: Correct — 30% of the 40% is 0.30 × 0.40 = 0.12, or 12% of all students.
why.D: This is the percent of band members in the choir, not the percent of all students.

context: A point is chosen at random inside the rectangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (0, 4). What is the probability that the point’s y-coordinate is less than its x-coordinate?

why.A: This assumes the line y = x cuts the rectangle in half, as it would a square. It leaves the rectangle through the top edge at (4, 4), not the corner.
why.B: This is the probability that y is greater than x, the region above the line.
why.C: This uses a triangle with legs 6 and 6, area 18, running past the top of the rectangle, which is only 4 tall.
why.D: Correct — the part of the rectangle above y = x is a triangle with vertices (0, 0), (4, 4) and (0, 4), of area 8. The other 24 − 8 = 16 square units lie below the line, and 16/24 = 2/3.

context: For a randomly chosen student, the probability of having a pet is 0.62, the probability of having a sibling is 0.75, and the probability of having both is 0.50. What is the probability that the student has neither a pet nor a sibling?

why.A: Correct — P(pet or sibling) = 0.62 + 0.75 − 0.50 = 0.87, so P(neither) = 1 − 0.87 = 0.13.
why.B: This is the probability of having a pet or a sibling or both, the complement of the answer.
why.C: This multiplies 0.38 by 0.25, assuming the events are independent. The given 0.50 shows they are not: 0.62 × 0.75 ≈ 0.47.
why.D: This is the probability of not having a pet, ignoring siblings.

context: Three fair coins are tossed. Given that at least one coin shows heads, what is the probability that at least two coins show heads?

why.A: This ignores the given condition and finds 4/8 over all 8 outcomes. Knowing there is a head rules out TTT.
why.B: Correct — 7 of the 8 outcomes have at least one head, and 4 of those (3 with exactly two heads, 1 with three) have at least two.
why.C: This counts only the outcomes with exactly two heads and leaves out HHH.
why.D: This is the unconditional probability of exactly two heads.

context: A committee of 4 people is chosen from 6 women and 4 men. How many different committees include at least one man?

why.A: This picks one man first, 4 ways, then any 3 of the other 9, 84 ways. A committee with two men is counted once for each of them.
why.B: This is the number of committees with no restriction.
why.C: Correct — there are C(10, 4) = 210 committees in all and C(6, 4) = 15 with no men, so 210 − 15 = 195 include a man.
why.D: This is the number of committees with no men, the ones to be removed.

context: A fish tank is a rectangular box 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 25 cm tall. When it is full, how many liters of water does it hold? (1 liter = 1,000 cubic centimeters)

why.A: This is the volume in cubic centimeters. It still has to be divided by 1,000 to give liters.
why.B: This divides the volume by 100 instead of 1,000.
why.C: This adds the three dimensions, 30 + 20 + 25, instead of multiplying them.
why.D: Correct — the volume is 30 × 20 × 25 = 15,000 cm³, and 15,000 ÷ 1,000 = 15 liters.

context: Landscaping soil is sold by the cubic yard, and 1 yard = 3 feet. How many cubic feet are in 1 cubic yard?

why.A: Correct — a cubic yard is a cube 3 feet on each edge, so it holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic feet.
why.B: This converts a length. A cubic yard has three dimensions, and each one is 3 feet.
why.C: This is the number of square feet in a square yard. A cubic yard has a third dimension.
why.D: This multiplies 3 by 27, applying the factor of 3 one time too many.

context: A figure is made of a rectangle 10 cm by 8 cm with a semicircle attached along one of its 8-cm sides. What is the area of the figure, in square centimeters?

why.A: This adds a whole circle of radius 4. Only half of it is attached.
why.B: Correct — the semicircle’s diameter is 8, so its radius is 4 and its area is ½ · π · 4² = 8π. Add the rectangle’s 80.
why.C: This uses the 8-cm side as the radius. The side is the diameter.
why.D: This adds the length of the curved edge, ½ · 2π · 4, instead of the area inside it.

context: A storage shed is a rectangular box 10 feet long, 8 feet wide and 6 feet tall, topped by a roof shaped like a triangular prism. Each triangular end of the roof has a base of 8 feet and a height of 3 feet, and the roof runs the full 10-foot length. What is the total volume of the shed, in cubic feet?

why.A: This counts the roof as a full box, leaving out the ½ in the triangle’s area. It is the same as a 10 × 8 × 9 box.
why.B: This is the box alone, without the roof.
why.C: Correct — the box holds 10 × 8 × 6 = 480, and the roof holds its end area, ½ × 8 × 3 = 12, times its 10-foot length, or 120.
why.D: This adds the area of one triangular end, 12, instead of the roof’s volume.

context: A cylindrical rain barrel has a radius of 3 feet and a height of 4 feet. One cubic foot holds about 7.5 gallons. To the nearest gallon, how many gallons does the barrel hold when full?

why.A: This leaves π out of the volume and multiplies 36 by 7.5.
why.B: This uses the diameter, 6, as the radius, which makes the volume four times too big.
why.C: This divides the volume by 7.5 instead of multiplying. Each cubic foot holds 7.5 gallons, so there are more gallons than cubic feet.
why.D: Correct — the volume is π · 3² · 4 = 36π ≈ 113.1 cubic feet, and 113.1 × 7.5 ≈ 848 gallons.

context: A model of a car is built at a scale of 1 : 24. The model’s windshield has an area of 15 square centimeters. What is the area of the real car’s windshield, in square centimeters?

why.A: Correct — lengths scale by 24, so areas scale by 24² = 576, and 15 × 576 = 8,640.
why.B: This scales the area by 24, the factor for lengths. Area grows by the square of the scale factor.
why.C: This scales by 24³, the factor for volume.
why.D: This doubles the scale factor, multiplying by 2 × 24, instead of squaring it.

context: A room is 12 feet wide and 15 feet long. Carpet is sold by the square yard, and 1 yard = 3 feet. How many square yards of carpet exactly cover the floor?

why.A: This divides the 180 square feet by 3. A square yard is 3 feet by 3 feet, or 9 square feet.
why.B: Correct — the room is 4 yards by 5 yards, so it needs 20 square yards. Equivalently, 180 square feet ÷ 9.
why.C: This is the area in square feet, not square yards.
why.D: This multiplies by 9 instead of dividing. A square yard is larger than a square foot, so there are fewer of them.

context: The three different faces of a rectangular box have areas of 12, 15 and 20 square inches. What is the volume of the box, in cubic inches?

why.A: This adds the three face areas. Volume is a product of the edges, not a sum of faces.
why.B: This multiplies the three face areas, which gives the square of the volume. It still needs a square root.
why.C: Correct — if the edges are a, b and c, then (ab)(ac)(bc) = (abc)² = 12 · 15 · 20 = 3,600, so abc = 60. The edges are 3, 4 and 5.
why.D: This finds the edges 3, 4 and 5 but adds them instead of multiplying.

context: A cone-shaped paper cup is held point down. Its rim has a radius of 3 cm, and it is 6 cm deep. Water fills it to a depth of 3 cm. What fraction of the cup’s volume is filled with water?

why.A: This assumes the water is half the volume because it reaches half the depth. The cone narrows toward the point.
why.B: This scales by the square of 1/2, as for an area. Volume scales by the cube.
why.C: This is the fraction of the cup that is still empty.
why.D: Correct — the water forms a smaller cone with every length half the cup’s, so its volume is (1/2)³ = 1/8 of the cup’s.

context: A goat is tied with a 10-meter rope to one outside corner of a rectangular shed that is 6 meters by 4 meters. The goat cannot enter the shed. Over what area, in square meters, can the goat graze?

why.A: Correct — the goat sweeps three quarters of a circle of radius 10, or 75π. Around the 6-meter side it has 4 meters of rope left, a quarter circle of 4π, and around the 4-meter side it has 6 meters left, a quarter circle of 9π.
why.B: This is a full circle of radius 10. The shed blocks a quarter of it.
why.C: This counts the three-quarter circle but not the areas the rope reaches after wrapping around the shed’s corners.
why.D: This lets the full 10-meter rope sweep a quarter circle past each corner. Part of the rope is used up along the shed’s side.

context: What is the area of a regular hexagon with sides of length 4?

why.A: This uses (√3/2) · s² for each triangle, leaving out the ½ from the triangle area formula.
why.B: Correct — the hexagon splits into 6 equilateral triangles with side 4, each of area (√3/4) · 4² = 4√3.
why.C: This splits the hexagon into only 3 equilateral triangles. It takes 6.
why.D: This uses 6 triangles but gives each a height of 4, the side length. The height of an equilateral triangle with side 4 is 2√3.

context: Kai jogs at a steady 6 miles per hour. How many minutes does it take him to jog 2.5 miles?

why.A: This multiplies the distance by the speed, 2.5 × 6. Time is distance divided by speed.
why.B: This divides the speed by the distance, 6 ÷ 2.5.
why.C: Correct — at 6 miles per hour he runs a mile every 10 minutes, so 2.5 miles take 25 minutes.
why.D: This is the time in hours, 2.5 ÷ 6. It still has to be converted to minutes.

context: A trail mix uses 2 cups of peanuts for every 3 cups of raisins. How many cups of raisins go with 12 cups of peanuts?

why.A: This turns the ratio around, treating 12 as the raisins’ share of 3.
why.B: This is the whole mix, peanuts and raisins together.
why.C: This adds the 1-cup difference between 2 and 3. A ratio scales by multiplying, not adding.
why.D: Correct — 12 cups of peanuts is 6 batches of 2 cups, and 6 × 3 = 18 cups of raisins.

context: A tank leaks water at 0.5 liters per minute. How many hours does it take the tank to lose 45 liters?

why.A: Correct — 45 ÷ 0.5 = 90 minutes, and 90 minutes is 1.5 hours.
why.B: This is the time in minutes. The question asks for hours.
why.C: This multiplies 45 by 0.5 instead of dividing.
why.D: This divides the 45 liters by 60 and ignores the leak rate.

context: In a 5-mile race, Priya runs the first 3 miles at an average of 8 minutes per mile. What average pace, in minutes per mile, must she run for the last 2 miles to finish in 38 minutes?

why.A: This is the average pace for the whole race, 38 ÷ 5. The first 3 miles were slower than that.
why.B: Correct — the first 3 miles take 24 minutes, which leaves 14 minutes for 2 miles, or 7 minutes per mile.
why.C: This is the time left for the last 2 miles, not the time per mile.
why.D: This divides the remaining 14 minutes by the 3 miles already run instead of the 2 still to go.

context: Four identical machines fill 1,200 bottles in 6 hours. At the same rate, how many hours would 6 of these machines take to fill 2,400 bottles?

why.A: This doubles the time for twice the bottles but ignores the two extra machines.
why.B: This adjusts only for the machines, 6 × 4/6, and forgets that there are twice as many bottles.
why.C: Correct — each machine fills 1,200 ÷ (4 × 6) = 50 bottles an hour, so 6 machines fill 300 an hour, and 2,400 ÷ 300 = 8.
why.D: This multiplies by 6/4 for the machines. More machines finish sooner, so that ratio should divide.

context: A leaky faucet drips once every 2 seconds, and 20 drops make 1 milliliter. How many liters of water does the faucet waste in one day?

why.A: This is the amount in milliliters. It still has to be divided by 1,000.
why.B: This counts a drop every second. The faucet drips once every 2 seconds.
why.C: This is the water wasted in one hour, not one day.
why.D: Correct — a day has 86,400 seconds, so 43,200 drops, which make 2,160 mL, or 2.16 liters.

context: A crew paved 40% of a road in 6 days. Working at the same rate, how many more days will the crew need to finish the road?

why.A: Correct — 40% took 6 days, so each 10% takes 1.5 days, and the remaining 60% takes 9 days.
why.B: This is the total time for the whole road. The crew has already worked 6 of those days.
why.C: This takes 60% of 6 days. The remaining work is bigger than the finished part, so it takes longer than 6 days.
why.D: This multiplies 6 by 40/60, the ratio upside down.

context: A 12-ounce glass of punch is 25% juice. How many ounces of the punch must be poured out and replaced with pure juice so that the glass is 50% juice?

why.A: This replaces just the 3 extra ounces of juice needed, forgetting that the punch poured out also held some juice.
why.B: Correct — pouring out x ounces removes 0.25x ounces of juice, and x ounces of juice go in, so 3 − 0.25x + x = 6. Then 0.75x = 3 and x = 4.
why.C: This adds juice without pouring any punch out, which would overflow a full glass.
why.D: This is how much of the original punch stays in the glass, not how much is poured out.

context: A car gets 30 miles per gallon, and gas costs $3.60 per gallon. What is the cost of gas for a 450-kilometer trip? (Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers.)

why.A: This multiplies by 1.6 to convert, which turns the trip into 720 miles. A mile is longer than a kilometer, so there are fewer miles.
why.B: This skips the conversion and treats 450 kilometers as 450 miles.
why.C: Correct — 450 km is 450 ÷ 1.6 = 281.25 miles, which uses 281.25 ÷ 30 = 9.375 gallons, costing 9.375 × $3.60 = $33.75.
why.D: This is the number of gallons, about 9.38, not the cost.

context: A cyclist rides for 30 minutes at 16 miles per hour and then for 45 minutes at 12 miles per hour. What is her average speed, in miles per hour, for the whole ride?

why.A: This averages the two speeds. She spent longer at 12 miles per hour, so the average is pulled toward 12.
why.B: This weights each speed by the other part’s time, 16 by 45 minutes and 12 by 30.
why.C: This is the total distance in miles. It still has to be divided by the 1.25 hours.
why.D: Correct — she covers 8 miles and then 9 miles, 17 miles in 1.25 hours, and 17 ÷ 1.25 = 13.6.

context: A phone’s battery starts the day fully charged. It uses 10% of a full charge for each hour the phone is in use and 2% for each hour it sits idle. Over a 12-hour day, the charge must never drop below 20%. What is the greatest whole number of hours the phone can be in use?

why.A: Correct — with u hours of use, the drain is 10u + 2(12 − u) = 8u + 24, and 8u + 24 ≤ 80 gives u ≤ 7.
why.B: This ignores the idle hours, 10u ≤ 80. The idle hours drain the battery too.
why.C: This charges the idle rate for all 12 hours, including the hours in use: 10u + 24 ≤ 80.
why.D: This lets the battery run all the way to 0%: 8u + 24 ≤ 100 gives u ≤ 9.5.

context: If g(t) = 10 − t², what is g(−3)?

why.A: This squares −3 to get −9. A negative number squared is positive.
why.B: Correct — (−3)² = 9, and 10 − 9 = 1.
why.C: This subtracts before squaring, (10 − (−3))². Only t is squared.
why.D: This forgets to square, computing 10 − (−3).

context: The graph of y = x² is stretched vertically by a factor of 3. Which point lies on the new graph?

why.A: This stretches the graph horizontally, tripling x instead of y.
why.B: This triples x before squaring, y = (3x)², which also shrinks the graph horizontally.
why.C: Correct — the new graph is y = 3x², so at x = 2 the y-value is 3 · 4 = 12.
why.D: This adds 3 to the y-value, which shifts the graph up instead of stretching it.

context: The graph of a function g is the line segment from (−3, 1) to (5, 9), including both endpoints. What is the range of g?

why.A: This is the domain, the set of x-values.
why.B: This mixes coordinates, pairing the first point’s y-value with the second point’s x-value.
why.C: This takes the smallest and largest numbers in the two points, mixing an x-value with a y-value.
why.D: Correct — the range is the set of y-values the graph reaches, from the lower endpoint’s 1 to the upper endpoint’s 9.

context: A graph shows the distance Lena has driven over time. It is a straight segment from (0 hours, 0 miles) to (2, 120), then a flat segment from (2, 120) to (3, 120), then a straight segment from (3, 120) to (5, 240). What was her average speed, in miles per hour, over the 5 hours?

why.A: Correct — she drove 240 miles in 5 hours, and 240 ÷ 5 = 48. The flat hour, when she was stopped, still counts.
why.B: This is her speed while moving, 240 miles over 4 hours. It leaves out the hour she was stopped.
why.C: This is the slope of the flat segment, her speed only while she was stopped.
why.D: This is the total distance. It still has to be divided by the time.

context: A linear function f has f(−1) = 7, f(1) = 3 and f(4) = −3. For what value of x is f(x) = 0?

why.A: This is f(0), the y-intercept. The question asks where the output is 0, not the input.
why.B: Correct — the slope is (3 − 7)/(1 − (−1)) = −2, so f(x) = −2x + 5, and −2x + 5 = 0 gives x = 2.5.
why.C: This solves −2x + 5 = 0 with a sign error, dividing −5 by −2 as if it gave a negative.
why.D: This divides the slope by the intercept, 2 ÷ 5, the ratio upside down.

context: The graph of y = f(x) has its highest point at (2, 5). What is the highest point of the graph of y = 3f(x) − 1?

why.A: This subtracts 1 before tripling, 3(5 − 1). The equation triples f(x) first.
why.B: This triples the x-coordinate too. Multiplying f(x) stretches the graph only vertically.
why.C: Correct — the transformation acts on outputs only, so x stays 2 and the y-value becomes 3(5) − 1 = 14.
why.D: This applies the shift but leaves out the factor of 3.

context: The graph of y = |x − 3| − 4 crosses the x-axis at two points. What is the distance between those points?

why.A: This is the distance from the vertex at x = 3 to one intercept. The two intercepts are on opposite sides.
why.B: This doubles the horizontal shift, 3, instead of the 4 that sets the intercepts.
why.C: This is the larger x-intercept, not the distance between the two.
why.D: Correct — |x − 3| = 4 gives x = 7 or x = −1, which are 8 units apart.

context: What is the average rate of change of f(x) = x² + 2x from x = 1 to x = 4?

why.A: Correct — f(4) = 24 and f(1) = 3, so the rate is (24 − 3)/(4 − 1) = 21/3 = 7.
why.B: This is the change in f. It still has to be divided by the change in x.
why.C: This divides by 4, the right endpoint, instead of the change in x, 4 − 1 = 3.
why.D: This divides f(4) by 4, using only one endpoint.

context: The function f(x) = (x − 1)² is defined only for −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. What is its range?

why.A: This evaluates only the endpoints, f(3) = 4 and f(−2) = 9, and misses the lower vertex between them.
why.B: Correct — the vertex at x = 1 lies inside the domain and gives the minimum 0. The farthest input from 1 is −2, which gives the maximum 9.
why.C: This is the range with no restriction on x. The domain stops at −2 and 3.
why.D: This uses the vertex and the right endpoint, but the left endpoint gives a larger value.

context: A function f is defined by f(1) = 3, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 1 and f(4) = 2. If g(x) = x + 2, for what value of x is f(g(x)) = 1?

why.A: This finds the input to f that gives 1, which is the value of g(x), but stops before solving for x.
why.B: This solves g(x) = 1 and skips f.
why.C: Correct — f gives 1 only when its input is 3, so g(x) = 3, and x + 2 = 3 gives x = 1.
why.D: This applies g to 3 instead of undoing it. g(x) = 3 means x + 2 = 3.

context: A function f is odd, meaning f(−x) = −f(x) for every x, and f(3) = 7. If g(x) = f(x) + 2, what is g(−3)?

why.A: This treats f as even, using f(−3) = 7.
why.B: This negates all of g(3) = 9. Only f is odd; the added 2 does not change sign.
why.C: This is f(−3). It still needs the 2 from g.

context: Through how many degrees does the minute hand of a clock turn from 2:10 to 2:35?

why.A: Correct — the minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, or 6° a minute, and 25 × 6 = 150.
why.B: This counts 1° for each minute. The hand covers 360° in 60 minutes, so it turns 6° a minute.
why.C: This is how far the hour hand turns in 25 minutes, at 0.5° a minute.
why.D: This uses 5° a minute, taking the 5 minutes between numbers as 5 degrees.

context: Lines AB and CD intersect at point E. Angle AEC measures (3x)° and angle BED measures (x + 40)°. What is the value of x?

why.A: This treats the angles as a linear pair, 3x + x + 40 = 180. Vertical angles are equal.
why.B: Correct — angles AEC and BED are vertical angles, so 3x = x + 40 and x = 20.
why.C: This is the measure of each angle, 3 × 20. The question asks for x.
why.D: This adds the x terms, 3x + x = 40, instead of moving x to one side.

context: Angles 1 and 2 are vertical angles, and angles 1 and 3 form a linear pair. If angle 2 measures 64°, what is the measure of angle 3?

why.A: This treats angle 3 as equal to angle 1. A linear pair adds to 180°.
why.B: This takes the complement, 90° − 64°. A linear pair makes a straight angle.
why.C: Correct — angle 1 equals angle 2, 64°, and angle 3 is its supplement, 180° − 64° = 116°.
why.D: This subtracts from 360°, the full turn around a point.

context: Parallel lines p and q are horizontal, with p above q, and point X lies between them. A segment runs up and to the left from X to point A on p, making a 30° angle with p on the right side of A. Another segment runs down and to the left from X to point B on q, making a 45° angle with q on the right side of B. What is the measure of angle AXB?

why.A: This is the supplement of the correct angle, 180° − 75°.
why.B: This subtracts the two given angles instead of adding them.
why.C: This is the reflex angle at X, measured the long way around.
why.D: Correct — a line through X parallel to p and q splits angle AXB into two alternate-interior copies, 30° and 45°.

context: From one vertex of a convex polygon, exactly 7 diagonals can be drawn. What is the sum of the polygon’s interior angles?

why.A: Correct — each vertex has diagonals to all but itself and its 2 neighbors, so n − 3 = 7 and n = 10. The sum is (10 − 2) × 180°.
why.B: This sets n − 2 = 7, giving 9 sides. A vertex has no diagonals to itself or its 2 neighbors, so subtract 3.
why.C: This finds 10 sides but multiplies 10 × 180° without subtracting 2.
why.D: This takes 7 as the number of sides, (7 − 2) × 180°.

context: Points A, B, C and D lie on a line in that order, with AB : BC : CD = 1 : 2 : 3 and AD = 36. What is the length of AC?

why.A: This is BC alone. AC runs from A through B to C.
why.B: Correct — the 6 parts cover 36, so each part is 6. AC is AB + BC, which is 3 parts, or 18.
why.C: This is AB, a single part.
why.D: This is BD, which is 2 + 3 = 5 parts.

context: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures 20°. What is the sum of its interior angles?

why.A: This finds 18 sides but multiplies 18 × 180° without subtracting 2.
why.B: This is one interior angle, 180° − 20°, not the sum of all 18.
why.D: This is the sum of the exterior angles, which is the same for every convex polygon.

context: In triangle ABC, angle A measures 70°. The bisectors of angles B and C meet at point I. What is the measure of angle BIC?

why.A: This is the sum of angles B and C. The bisectors take only half of each.
why.B: This is the sum of the two half-angles at B and C, not the third angle of triangle BIC.
why.C: This bisects angle A instead, 180° − 35°. The bisectors meeting at I come from B and C.
why.D: Correct — angles B and C add to 110°, so their halves add to 55°, and angle BIC = 180° − 55° = 125°.

context: The sides of a regular pentagon are extended until they meet, forming a five-pointed star. What is the measure of the angle at each point of the star?

why.A: Correct — each point sits on a triangle whose base angles are exterior angles of the pentagon, 72° each, so the point is 180° − 144° = 36°.
why.B: This is an exterior angle of the pentagon, one of the base angles of the point’s triangle.
why.C: This is an interior angle of the pentagon.
why.D: This treats each point of the star as part of an equilateral triangle.

context: The interior angles of a convex polygon add up to 2,340°. How many diagonals does the polygon have?

why.A: This multiplies 15 × 12 without halving. Each diagonal has two ends, so it is counted twice.
why.B: Correct — 2,340 ÷ 180 = 13, so n = 15. Each vertex has 12 diagonals, and 15 × 12 counts each diagonal twice, giving 90.
why.C: This counts every pair of vertices, 15 × 14 ÷ 2, which includes the 15 sides.
why.D: This is the number of diagonals from one vertex.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. Point D lies on side AC so that AD = BD = BC. What is the measure of angle A?

why.A: This is angle ABC or angle C, the base angles of triangle ABC.
why.B: This is angle ADB, the angle at D inside triangle ABD.
why.C: Correct — if angle A = x, then angle ABD = x, the exterior angle BDC = 2x, angle C = 2x since BD = BC, and angle ABC = 2x since AB = AC. So 5x = 180.
why.D: This treats triangle ABC as equilateral. Only two of its sides are equal.

context: Cans are stacked in layers. The bottom layer has 20 cans, and each layer above it has 2 fewer cans than the layer below it. How many cans are in the 7th layer from the bottom?

why.A: This subtracts 2 seven times. The bottom layer is the 1st, so only 6 steps separate it from the 7th.
why.B: This adds 2 for each layer. The layers get smaller going up.
why.C: This is the total decrease from the bottom layer, not the number of cans left in the 7th.
why.D: Correct — the 7th layer is 6 layers above the bottom, so it has 20 − 6 × 2 = 8 cans.

context: A sequence is defined by aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1. What is the 5th term?

why.A: Correct — 2⁵ = 32, and 32 − 1 = 31.
why.B: This multiplies 2 by 5 instead of raising 2 to the 5th power.
why.C: This computes 2⁵ but leaves off the − 1.
why.D: This is the 4th term, 2⁴ − 1.

context: An arithmetic sequence has a first term of 5 and a common difference of −3. Which expression gives its nth term?

why.A: This takes n steps from the first term. The 1st term is 0 steps from itself, so the count is n − 1. This formula gives 2 when n = 1.
why.B: Correct — the nth term is 5 + (n − 1)(−3) = 5 − 3n + 3 = 8 − 3n. Check: n = 1 gives 5.
why.C: This adds the difference instead of subtracting it, 5 + 3(n − 1).
why.D: This swaps the roles of the first term and the difference.

context: A row of squares is built from toothpicks. One square uses 4 toothpicks, and each square added to the end of the row uses 3 more. Which expression gives the number of toothpicks in a row of n squares?

why.A: This gives every square 4 toothpicks of its own. Neighboring squares share a side.
why.B: This swaps the roles of n and 3, adding 1 per square instead of 3.
why.C: Correct — the first square uses 4 and each of the other n − 1 squares adds 3, so 4 + 3(n − 1) = 3n + 1.
why.D: This starts from 4 and then adds 3 for every square, counting the first square twice.

context: A town’s population was 800, 1,200, 1,800 and 2,700 in four consecutive decades. If the pattern continues, what will the population be in the next decade?

why.A: This adds the last increase, 900, again. The increases themselves grow, so the pattern is multiplicative.
why.B: This doubles the last value. The ratio between terms is 1.5, not 2.
why.C: This is the next increase, 900 × 1.5, not the next population.
why.D: Correct — each value is 1.5 times the one before (1,200 ÷ 800 = 1.5), and 2,700 × 1.5 = 4,050.

context: The sum of 9 consecutive even integers is 450. What is the largest of the 9 integers?

why.A: Correct — the middle (5th) number is the mean, 450 ÷ 9 = 50. The largest is 4 steps of 2 above it, 50 + 8 = 58.
why.B: This is the middle number, the mean of the 9, not the largest.
why.C: This adds 8 steps of 2 to the middle number. The middle is the 5th number, only 4 steps below the 9th.
why.D: This adds 4 steps of 1, as for consecutive integers. Consecutive even integers are 2 apart.

context: The numbers 3, x, 12 form a geometric sequence with x > 0, and the numbers 3, y, 12 form an arithmetic sequence. What is x + y?

why.A: This treats both sequences as arithmetic, 7.5 + 7.5.
why.B: Correct — geometric means x² = 3 × 12 = 36, so x = 6. Arithmetic means y = (3 + 12)/2 = 7.5. The sum is 13.5.
why.C: This treats both sequences as geometric, 6 + 6.
why.D: This is y − x, the difference between the two means, not their sum.

context: Sequence P is 5, 12, 19, … and sequence Q is 89, 84, 79, …. For one value of n, the nth term of P equals the nth term of Q. What is that common value?

why.A: This is the term number n, not the value of the terms.
why.B: This finds n = 8 but adds 8 steps of 7 to the first term of P. The 8th term is only 7 steps past the 1st.
why.C: Correct — 5 + 7(n − 1) = 89 − 5(n − 1) gives 12(n − 1) = 84, so n = 8, and the 8th term of each is 54.
why.D: This finds n = 8 but subtracts 8 steps of 5 from the first term of Q. The 8th term is only 7 steps past the 1st.

context: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 2 and aₙ₊₁ = 1/(1 − aₙ) for n ≥ 1. What is a₁₀₀?

why.A: This is a₂. It lines 100 up with the second place in the cycle.
why.B: This is a₃, the term at 99, a multiple of 3. The 100th term is one place further.
why.C: This is the sum of one full cycle, 2 + (−1) + 1/2, not a single term.
why.D: Correct — the terms run 2, −1, 1/2, 2, −1, 1/2, …, repeating every 3. Since 100 = 99 + 1, a₁₀₀ matches a₁.

context: Under Plan A, a job pays $100 in week 1 and $20 more each week than the week before. Under Plan B, it pays $2 in week 1 and doubles its pay each week. In which week does Plan B’s pay first exceed Plan A’s?

why.A: Correct — in week n Plan A pays 100 + 20(n − 1) and Plan B pays 2ⁿ. In week 7 that is $220 against $128, and in week 8 it is $240 against $256.
why.B: This uses 100 + 20n for Plan A, adding a raise in week 1. Then week 8 is $260 against $256.
why.C: This uses 2ⁿ⁻¹ for Plan B, as if it started at $1. Plan B pays $2 in week 1, so its pay in week n is 2ⁿ.
why.D: This compares Plan B with a flat $100 and ignores Plan A’s weekly raises: 2⁷ = 128.

context: A geometric sequence has a first term of 3 and a common ratio of 2. What is the least number of terms whose sum is greater than 1,000?

why.A: This finds when a single term, 3 · 2ⁿ⁻¹, passes 1,000. The question is about the sum of the terms.
why.B: Correct — the sum of n terms is 3(2ⁿ − 1). For n = 8 that is 765, and for n = 9 it is 1,533.
why.C: This is the last n whose sum, 765, is still below 1,000, not the first one above it.
why.D: This treats the sequence as adding 3 each time, so that 3n > 1,000.

context: A circular running track has a circumference of 400 meters. To the nearest meter, what is its diameter?

why.A: This divides by 2π, which gives the radius, about 63.7 meters.
why.B: This multiplies 400 by π instead of dividing.
why.C: Correct — circumference is π times the diameter, so d = 400 ÷ π ≈ 127.3 meters.
why.D: This halves the circumference, as if the diameter were half the distance around.

context: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle, and side AB is a diameter of the circle. If angle A measures 35°, what is the measure of angle B?

why.A: This is angle C, the angle that faces the diameter.
why.B: This treats the triangle as isosceles with angle B equal to angle A. Nothing makes those two sides equal.
why.C: This doubles angle A, as if it were a central angle.
why.D: Correct — an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle, so angle C = 90°, and angle B = 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°.

context: Two circles have radii of 3 and 5. They touch at exactly one point, and neither circle is inside the other. What is the distance between their centers?

why.A: Correct — the point of contact lies on the segment joining the centers, so the distance is 3 + 5.
why.B: This subtracts the radii, which fits one circle touching the other from inside.
why.C: This adds the two diameters. Each center is only one radius from the point of contact.
why.D: This treats the two radii as legs of a right triangle. They lie along one straight line.

context: From point P outside a circle, two tangent segments touch the circle at A and B. If PA = 3x + 2 and PB = 5x − 6, what is the length of PA?

why.A: This is the value of x, not the length of PA.
why.B: Correct — tangent segments from the same outside point are equal, so 3x + 2 = 5x − 6, which gives x = 4 and PA = 14.
why.C: This is PA + PB, the two tangent segments together.
why.D: This comes from a sign slip, 2x = 4 instead of 2x = 8, so x = 2 and 3(2) + 2 = 8.

context: A rider sits at the edge of a merry-go-round with a radius of 6 meters. The merry-go-round makes one full turn every 12 seconds. What is the rider’s speed, in meters per second?

why.A: This is the distance for one full turn. It still has to be divided by the 12 seconds.
why.B: This divides the area of the circle, 36π, by 12. The rider travels along the circumference.
why.C: Correct — one turn carries the rider around the circumference, 2π · 6 = 12π meters, in 12 seconds, which is π meters per second.
why.D: This uses 6 as the diameter, which halves the circumference.

context: A sector of a circle has a radius of 9 and a central angle of 80°. What is the perimeter of the sector?

why.A: This is the arc alone. The sector’s boundary also includes two radii.
why.B: This includes only one of the two radii.
why.C: This adds the sector’s area, 80/360 of 81π, instead of the arc length.
why.D: Correct — the arc is 80/360 of 2π · 9, which is 4π, and the sector’s boundary also includes two radii of 9.

context: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle. Angle A measures (2x + 10)° and angle C measures (3x + 20)°. What is the measure of angle A?

why.A: Correct — opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary, so 5x + 30 = 180, x = 30 and angle A = 70°.
why.B: This is angle C, the angle opposite A.
why.C: This is the value of x, not the angle.
why.D: This assumes every angle of an inscribed quadrilateral is a right angle. Only the opposite pairs are tied, adding to 180°.

context: From point P outside a circle, a tangent touches the circle at T. A secant from P meets the circle first at A and then at B, with PA = 4 and AB = 5. What is the length of PT?

why.A: This multiplies PA by the chord AB, 4 × 5. The product uses the whole secant, PB = 9.
why.B: Correct — the tangent squared equals the whole secant times its outside part: PT² = PA · PB = 4 × 9 = 36.
why.C: This treats PA and AB as the legs of a right triangle.
why.D: This is PB, the whole secant, not the tangent.

context: Two circles have radii of 5 and 3, and their centers are 10 units apart. A line is tangent to both circles, and both circles lie on the same side of the line. What is the distance between the two points of tangency?

why.A: This uses the sum of the radii, 5 + 3, which fits a tangent that passes between the circles.
why.B: This is the distance between the centers.
why.C: Correct — the radii to the tangent line are both perpendicular to it, so the tangent segment is a leg of a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and other leg 5 − 3 = 2: √(100 − 4) = √96.
why.D: This adds the squares, √(100 + 4), treating the 10 as a leg instead of the hypotenuse.

context: The line y = x + 1 crosses the circle x² + y² = 25 at two points. What is the distance between those two points?

why.A: This is the difference in x-coordinates alone. The points also differ by 7 in y.
why.B: This is the diameter. The line does not pass through the center (0, 0).
why.C: This uses 1, the line’s y-intercept, as its distance from the center. The perpendicular distance from (0, 0) to the line is 1/√2.
why.D: Correct — substituting gives x² + x − 12 = 0, so x = 3 or x = −4, giving (3, 4) and (−4, −3), which are √(49 + 49) = 7√2 apart.

context: Points A, B and C lie on a circle. Minor arc AB measures 100°, minor arc BC measures 120°, and the two arcs do not overlap. What is the measure of angle ABC?

why.A: Correct — angle ABC intercepts arc AC, the part not containing B, which is 360° − 100° − 120° = 140°, and an inscribed angle is half its arc.
why.B: This takes half of the two given arcs, (100° + 120°)/2. Angle B intercepts the arc opposite it, not the arcs next to it.
why.C: This is the intercepted arc itself. The inscribed angle is half of it.
why.D: This takes half of arc BC. Angle B intercepts arc AC.

context: Which of the following points satisfies both y > x and y < 4?

why.A: Here y = 1 is less than x = 3, so the first condition fails. This swaps the coordinates.
why.B: Correct — 3 > 1 and 3 < 4, so the point meets both conditions.
why.C: This meets y > x, but y = 5 is not less than 4.
why.D: This meets y > x, but y = 6 is not less than 4. Checking only the first condition is not enough.

context: The graphs of the two equations in a system of linear equations are distinct parallel lines. How many solutions does the system have?

why.A: This is the case for lines with different slopes, which cross at one point.
why.B: This is the case when the two equations describe the same line.
why.C: Correct — a solution is a point on both lines, and distinct parallel lines never meet.
why.D: Two straight lines cannot cross twice. That can happen only when one of the graphs is curved.

context: Line k passes through (0, 1) and (2, 7). At what point does line k intersect the line y = −x + 13?

why.A: This solves 3x + 1 = 13 with only one x term, dropping the −x from the second line.
why.B: This finds the right values but swaps the coordinates.
why.C: This is a point on line k, but it is not on y = −x + 13.
why.D: Correct — line k has slope 6/2 = 3 and equation y = 3x + 1. Then 3x + 1 = −x + 13 gives x = 3, and y = 10.

context: A bakery spends $240 a day on fixed costs plus $1.50 to make each loaf, and it sells each loaf for $4.50. How many loaves must it sell in a day for its income to equal its costs?

why.A: Correct — setting 4.50n = 240 + 1.50n gives 3n = 240, so n = 80. Each loaf covers $3 of the fixed costs.
why.B: This divides the fixed costs by the $1.50 cost per loaf. Each loaf contributes its price minus its cost, $3.
why.C: This divides the fixed costs by the $4.50 price, ignoring what each loaf costs to make.
why.D: This divides by the price plus the cost, $6. The cost per loaf reduces what each sale contributes.

context: The digits of a two-digit number add to 11. When the digits are reversed, the new number is 27 more than the original. What is the original number?

why.A: This is the reversed number, 27 more than the original.
why.B: Correct — with tens digit a and units digit b, a + b = 11 and (10b + a) − (10a + b) = 9(b − a) = 27, so b − a = 3. Then a = 4 and b = 7.
why.C: This is the difference between the digits, b − a.
why.D: This is the units digit alone, not the whole number.

context: Pipes A and B together fill a tank in 6 hours. Pipe A fills water twice as fast as pipe B. How many hours would pipe B take to fill the tank alone?

why.A: This is the time for pipe A alone, the faster pipe.
why.B: This doubles the time for both pipes together. Removing A leaves only a third of the combined rate, not half.
why.C: Correct — if B fills r of the tank per hour, A fills 2r, and together 3r = 1/6, so r = 1/18. B alone takes 18 hours.
why.D: This halves the combined time. A single pipe must take longer than both together.

context: A linear function f has f(0) = 3 and f(2) = 7. A linear function g has g(0) = 15 and g(3) = 9. For what value of x is f(x) = g(x)?

why.A: This is the common output, f(3) = g(3) = 9, not the input.
why.B: This adds the intercepts, 3 + 15 = 18, instead of subtracting, and divides by 4.
why.C: This solves 2x = 12, forgetting to collect both x terms on one side.
why.D: Correct — f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = 15 − 2x, so 2x + 3 = 15 − 2x gives 4x = 12 and x = 3.

context: How many points (x, y) with integer coordinates satisfy all three of x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 and x + 2y ≤ 6?

why.A: Correct — for y = 0, 1, 2 and 3, x can run from 0 up to 6, 4, 2 and 0, giving 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16 points.
why.B: This leaves out the 4 points on the line x + 2y = 6. The ≤ includes them.
why.C: This is the area of the triangle, ½ × 6 × 3, not a count of points.
why.D: This counts every point of the 7-by-4 rectangle, including the ones above the line.

context: If x² + y² = 25 and x + y = 7, what is the value of xy?

why.A: This finds 2xy = 24 but does not divide by 2.
why.B: Correct — (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y², so 49 = 25 + 2xy, which gives xy = 12.
why.C: This subtracts in the wrong order, 25 − 49 = 2xy.
why.D: This adds 49 and 25. The identity makes 49 exceed 25 by 2xy.

context: A caterer charges a fixed fee plus the same amount per guest. A party of 40 guests costs $1,100, and a party of 60 guests costs $1,500. What does a party of 75 guests cost?

why.A: This scales the 40-guest price in proportion, 1,100 × 75/40, which charges the fixed fee again for every guest.
why.B: This scales the 60-guest price in proportion, 1,500 × 75/60, which also scales the fixed fee.
why.C: Correct — 20 more guests cost $400 more, so each guest costs $20, and the fee is 1,100 − 40 × 20 = $300. Then 300 + 75 × 20 = $1,800.
why.D: This is 75 guests at $20 each, leaving out the $300 fee.

context: The point (x, y) must satisfy x + y ≤ 10, y ≥ 2x − 2, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. What is the greatest possible value of 3x + y?

why.A: This uses (10, 0), which meets x + y ≤ 10 but breaks y ≥ 2x − 2.
why.B: This uses the corner (0, 10), which gives the largest y but not the largest 3x + y.
why.C: This finds the corner (4, 6) but evaluates only 3x, dropping the y.
why.D: Correct — the region’s corners are (0, 0), (1, 0), (4, 6) and (0, 10). At (4, 6), 3x + y = 18, the largest of 0, 3, 18 and 10.

context: How many points does the graph of y = (x − 4)² have in common with the x-axis?

why.A: Correct — y = 0 only when x − 4 = 0, so the graph touches the x-axis at the single point (4, 0), its vertex.
why.B: This counts the two factors of (x − 4)(x − 4) as two points. Both give the same x, 4.
why.C: This assumes a squared expression is always positive. It equals 0 when x = 4.
why.D: This gives the x-coordinate of the point, not the number of points.

context: The height, in feet, of a ball t seconds after it is thrown is h(t) = −16t² + 32t + 6. What is the ball’s height after 1 second?

why.A: This drops the negative sign on −16t², adding 16 instead of subtracting it.
why.C: This is the height at t = 0, when the ball is thrown.
why.D: This subtracts the 32t term instead of adding it.

context: A quadratic function f has f(0) = 3, f(1) = 2 and f(2) = 3. What is f(4)?

why.A: This continues in a straight line from the last two values, rising 1 per step. A quadratic’s changes grow.
why.B: This mirrors f(0) about x = 2. The axis of symmetry is x = 1, halfway between 0 and 2.
why.C: Correct — the equal values at x = 0 and x = 2 put the vertex at x = 1, so f(x) = (x − 1)² + 2, and f(4) = 9 + 2 = 11.
why.D: This puts the vertex at (2, 3), using f(x) = (x − 2)² + 3.

context: What is the value of 51² − 49²?

why.A: This squares the difference, (51 − 49)². The difference of squares is (a − b)(a + b), not (a − b)².
why.B: This is a + b alone, leaving out the factor a − b = 2.
why.C: This is a − b alone, leaving out the factor a + b = 100.
why.D: Correct — a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) = 2 × 100 = 200.

context: The graph of a quadratic function touches the x-axis only at x = 3 and crosses the y-axis at y = 18. Which equation describes the graph?

why.A: Correct — touching the axis only at 3 means y = a(x − 3)², and x = 0 gives 9a = 18, so a = 2.
why.B: This flips the sign inside the square, which moves the vertex to x = −3.
why.C: This uses the y-intercept as a. At x = 0 that gives 18 × 9 = 162.
why.D: This makes the y-intercept 18 by adding 9, but that lifts the vertex off the x-axis.

context: The shape of an arch is modeled by y = −0.1(x − 20)² + 40, where x and y are in feet and the arch meets the ground where y = 0. How wide is the arch at ground level, in feet?

why.A: This is the distance from the center, x = 20, to one end. The arch reaches as far on the other side.
why.B: Correct — 0.1(x − 20)² = 40 gives (x − 20)² = 400, so x = 0 or x = 40, which are 40 feet apart.
why.C: This is (x − 20)², before taking the square root.
