why.D: This doubles the height of 40. The width comes from the x-intercepts, not the peak.

context: A company’s monthly profit, in dollars, from selling x hundred units is P(x) = −2(x − 15)² + 450. For which values of x is the profit at least $400?

why.A: This keeps the direction of the inequality when dividing by −2. Dividing by a negative flips it.
why.B: This takes only the positive square root, x − 15 ≤ 5, and starts from the peak.
why.C: Correct — −2(x − 15)² + 450 ≥ 400 gives (x − 15)² ≤ 25, so x − 15 is between −5 and 5.
why.D: This solves for x − 15 and forgets to add the 15 back.

context: A farmer has 60 meters of fencing to enclose a rectangular pen against a long barn wall, so only three sides need fencing. What is the greatest area, in square meters, the pen can have?

why.A: This makes the three fenced sides equal, 20 each. The side along the wall can be longer.
why.B: This fences all four sides with the 60 meters, a 15-by-15 square. The wall saves one side.
why.C: This is the length of the side parallel to the wall, not the area.
why.D: Correct — with sides x meters from the wall, the area is x(60 − 2x), which peaks at x = 15, giving 15 × 30 = 450.

context: The solutions of x² − 5x + 3 = 0 are r and s. What is the value of r² + s²?

why.A: Correct — r + s = 5 and rs = 3, so r² + s² = (r + s)² − 2rs = 25 − 6 = 19.
why.B: This squares the sum, (r + s)², which also includes 2rs.
why.C: This adds 2rs instead of subtracting it.
why.D: This subtracts rs once instead of twice.

context: The graph of y = x² − 6x + k crosses the x-axis at two points that are 4 units apart. What is the value of k?

why.A: This puts each crossing 4 units from the axis. The two crossings are 4 apart, so each is 2 from the axis.
why.B: Correct — the crossings are centered on the axis x = 3, so they are x = 1 and x = 5, and k is their product, 5.
why.C: This makes the graph touch the x-axis once, at x = 3, instead of crossing it twice.
why.D: This subtracts the half-distance, 9 − 2, without squaring it. The crossings solve (x − 3)² = 9 − k = 4.

context: Which describes all values of x for which x² < 4x?

why.A: This divides both sides by x, which is allowed only for positive x. Negative x, such as x = −1, fail.
why.B: This is where x(x − 4) is positive, the opposite of what is asked.
why.C: Correct — x² − 4x < 0 means x(x − 4) < 0, which holds when x is between the zeros 0 and 4.
why.D: This solves x² < 4, dropping the x from the right side.

context: Angle θ is drawn in standard position, and its terminal side crosses the unit circle at (−0.6, 0.8). What is cos θ?

why.A: This is the y-coordinate, which is sin θ.
why.B: This divides x by y, which gives cot θ, not cos θ.
why.C: This drops the sign. The point is left of the y-axis, so cos θ is negative.
why.D: Correct — on the unit circle, the x-coordinate of the point is cos θ.

context: In a circle with a radius of 5, a central angle of 2 radians intercepts an arc. What is the length of the arc?

why.A: Correct — a radian measure is arc length divided by radius, so the arc is 5 × 2 = 10.
why.B: This divides the radius by the angle. Arc length is radius times angle in radians.
why.C: This treats 2 radians as 2π radians, a full turn.
why.D: This is the area of the sector, ½ · 5² · 2, not the arc length.

context: Which of the following angles has the same sine as 40°?

why.A: This is the complement of 40°. sin 50° equals cos 40°, not sin 40°.
why.B: Correct — angles θ and 180° − θ have the same height on the unit circle, so sin 140° = sin 40°.
why.C: This adds 180°, which lands in quadrant III, where the sine is negative.
why.D: This reflects 40° across the x-axis, which flips the sign of the sine.

context: For 0 ≤ θ < 2π, sin θ = −1/2 and θ lies in quadrant IV. What is θ?

why.A: This is the quadrant III angle with sine −1/2, π + π/6.
why.B: This is the reference angle, in quadrant I, where the sine is positive.
why.C: Correct — the reference angle for sine 1/2 is π/6, and in quadrant IV the angle is 2π − π/6 = 11π/6.
why.D: This uses the reference angle π/3, which belongs to a cosine of 1/2, not a sine of 1/2.

context: For an acute angle x, sin x = cos(2x − 30°), where 2x − 30° is also acute. What is x?

why.A: This sets the two angles equal, x = 2x − 30°. Sine and cosine agree on complementary angles, not equal ones.
why.B: This makes the two angles supplementary, 3x − 30° = 180°.
why.C: This finds x = 40° but reports the other angle, 2x − 30°.
why.D: Correct — the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement, so x + (2x − 30°) = 90°, and 3x = 120°.

context: Angle θ is drawn in standard position with measure 5π/4 radians. At what point does its terminal side cross the unit circle?

why.A: Correct — 5π/4 is π/4 past π, in quadrant III, where both coordinates are negative, each √2/2 in size.
why.B: This is the point for π/4, in quadrant I. The signs must match quadrant III.
why.C: This is the point for 3π/4, in quadrant II.
why.D: This is the point for 4π/3, which uses a reference angle of π/3 instead of π/4.

context: Which angle from 0° up to 360° is coterminal with −500°?

why.A: This subtracts 360° from 500° and drops the negative sign. −500° turns clockwise.
why.B: Correct — adding 360° twice gives −500° + 720° = 220°.
why.C: This adds 360° only once. The result is still negative, so another 360° is needed.
why.D: This is the reference angle of 220°, not a coterminal angle.

context: How many solutions does 2cos²x − cos x − 1 = 0 have for 0 ≤ x < 2π?

why.A: This counts only the solutions of cos x = −1/2 and misses x = 0 from cos x = 1.
why.B: This counts both 0 and 2π. The interval stops before 2π.
why.C: Correct — the equation factors as (2cos x + 1)(cos x − 1) = 0. cos x = 1 gives x = 0, and cos x = −1/2 gives 2π/3 and 4π/3.
why.D: This finds one angle for each of the two cosine values, but cos x = −1/2 has two.

context: In triangle ABC, a = 6, b = 10 and angle A = 30°, where side a is opposite angle A and side b is opposite angle B. How many different triangles fit these measurements?

why.A: This takes only the acute value of B. The obtuse angle 180° − 56° also works because 30° + 124° < 180°.
why.B: This assumes no triangle exists because a is shorter than b. The height b sin A = 5 is less than 6, so side a reaches the base.
why.C: Two sides and an angle fix at most two triangles.
why.D: Correct — sin B = 10 · sin 30° / 6 = 5/6, so B is about 56° or about 124°, and both leave room for angle C.

context: Angle θ lies in quadrant II and sin θ = 0.6. What is cos(π + θ)?

why.A: Correct — in quadrant II cos θ = −0.8, and cos(π + θ) = −cos θ = 0.8.
why.B: This is cos θ itself. Adding π reverses the sign of the cosine.
why.C: This uses the sine value, 0.6, instead of the cosine.
why.D: This negates the sine. cos(π + θ) depends on cos θ, not sin θ.

context: What is the period of y = sin(3x) + cos(2x)?

why.A: This takes the longer of the two periods. After π, sin(3x) is only partway through a cycle.
why.B: Correct — the terms have periods 2π/3 and π, and the smallest length that is a whole number of both is 2π, which is 3 and 2 of them.
why.C: This adds the two periods. The sum repeats only when both terms repeat together.
why.D: This multiplies 3 × 2 and then by π. The least common multiple of 2π/3 and π is smaller.

context: The pH of a solution is −log[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the hydrogen-ion concentration and log is the base-10 logarithm. What is the pH of a solution with [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵?

why.A: This is log[H⁺] itself. The formula takes its negative.
why.B: This computes 10⁵, undoing a logarithm instead of taking one.
why.C: Correct — log(10⁻⁵) = −5, and the formula’s minus sign makes the pH 5.
why.D: This reports the base of the logarithm, not the exponent.

context: For every positive x, log(1/x) can be rewritten as which expression?

why.A: This takes the reciprocal of the logarithm. The reciprocal inside becomes a minus sign outside.
why.B: This uses the quotient rule but takes log 1 as 1. Since 10⁰ = 1, log 1 = 0.
why.C: This moves the minus sign onto x. A negative input has no real logarithm.
why.D: Correct — log(1/x) = log 1 − log x = 0 − log x.

context: What value of x satisfies 5 · 2ˣ = 40?

why.A: Correct — dividing by 5 gives 2ˣ = 8 = 2³.
why.B: This is the value of 2ˣ. It still has to be written as a power of 2.
why.C: This subtracts 5 instead of dividing, solving 2ˣ = 35.
why.D: This solves 10ˣ = 8, using base 10 instead of base 2.

context: If log₃(x²) = 4 and x > 0, what is x?

why.A: This is x², not x. It still needs a square root.
why.B: Correct — x² = 3⁴ = 81, so x = 9. Equivalently, 2 log₃ x = 4 gives log₃ x = 2.
why.C: This is log₃ x, not x.
why.D: This multiplies 4 by 3 instead of raising 3 to the 4th power.

context: To the nearest hundredth, what is log₃ 50?

why.A: This divides 50 by 3. The logarithm asks for an exponent.
why.B: This is log 50 in base 10, before dividing by log 3.
why.C: Correct — by the change of base rule, log₃ 50 = log 50 / log 3 ≈ 1.699 / 0.477 ≈ 3.56. Check: 3³ = 27 and 3⁴ = 81.
why.D: This divides upside down, log 3 / log 50.

context: Which single logarithm is equal to 3 + 2 log₂ x for every positive x?

why.A: This puts the 3 inside the logarithm as it stands. The 3 must first be written as log₂ 8.
why.B: This turns a sum of logarithms into the logarithm of a sum. Adding logarithms multiplies their arguments.
why.C: This squares the 8 along with x. The coefficient 2 applies only to log₂ x.
why.D: Correct — 3 = log₂ 8 and 2 log₂ x = log₂ x², and a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product.

context: If log₂ x = 3 + log₂ 5, what is the value of x?

why.A: Correct — 3 = log₂ 8, so log₂ x = log₂ 8 + log₂ 5 = log₂ 40.
why.B: This adds 8 and 5. A sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product.
why.C: This multiplies 3 by 5, treating 3 as the number instead of log₂ 8.
why.D: This adds 3 and 5 as exponents, 2³⁺⁵. Only the 3 is an exponent of 2.

context: To the nearest hundredth, what value of x satisfies 2ˣ⁺³ = 5ˣ?

why.A: This drops the x log 2 term, solving x log 5 = 3 log 2.
why.B: Correct — taking logarithms, (x + 3) log 2 = x log 5, so x(log 5 − log 2) = 3 log 2 and x = 3 log 2 / (log 5 − log 2) ≈ 2.27.
why.C: This treats the bases as ordinary numbers, 3/(5 − 2).
why.D: This subtracts the logarithms in the wrong order, log 2 − log 5.

context: If log₄ x + log₂ x = 6, what is x?

why.A: This treats log₄ x as log₂ x, so 2 log₂ x = 6.
why.B: This drops the log₄ x term and solves log₂ x = 6.
why.C: Correct — log₄ x = ½ log₂ x, so 1.5 log₂ x = 6, log₂ x = 4 and x = 16.
why.D: This is log₂ x, not x.

context: If log_a b = 3, where a and b are positive and not 1, what is log_b(a²)?

why.A: This multiplies 2 by 3 without switching the base. log_b a is the reciprocal of log_a b.
why.B: This takes the reciprocal of the whole product 2 × 3. Only log_a b is inverted.
why.C: This puts the 2 in the denominator. The exponent multiplies the logarithm.
why.D: Correct — log_b a = 1/3 because the two logarithms are reciprocals, and log_b(a²) = 2 · 1/3.

context: If 3ᵃ = 5 and 5ᵇ = 9, what is the value of ab?

why.A: Correct — 3ᵃᵇ = (3ᵃ)ᵇ = 5ᵇ = 9 = 3², so ab = 2.
why.B: This multiplies the numbers 5 and 9. The product ab is an exponent.
why.C: This divides 9 by 5.
why.D: This is the base that ties the equations together, not the product of the exponents.

context: What is 0.6% written as a decimal?

why.A: This moves the decimal point only one place. Dividing by 100 moves it two places.
why.B: This drops the percent sign without dividing by 100.
why.C: This multiplies by 100 instead of dividing, the conversion from a decimal to a percent run the wrong way.
why.D: Correct — percent means “per hundred,” so 0.6% = 0.6 ÷ 100 = 0.006.

context: A phone battery holds 3,500 milliampere-hours (mAh) when full, and its display reads 64%. How many mAh of charge are left?

why.B: This is 36% of 3,500, the charge already used rather than the charge left.
why.C: This divides 3,500 by 0.64. Finding a percent of a whole multiplies.
why.D: This uses 6.4% instead of 64%, a decimal point one place too far left.

context: Two-thirds of the members of a hiking club are students, and three-fourths of those students are in their first year. What fraction of the whole club are first-year students?

why.A: This adds the numerators and the denominators, (2 + 3)/(3 + 4), which is not an operation on fractions.
why.B: Correct — “three-fourths of” the two-thirds means multiplying: (3/4)(2/3) = 6/12 = 1/2.
why.C: This subtracts, 3/4 − 2/3. A fraction “of” a group multiplies.
why.D: This adds the two fractions, which gives more than the whole club.

context: The share of a city’s electricity that comes from solar power rose from 8% to 12%. Which statement describes the change correctly?

choices.text: It rose 4 percentage points, a 4% increase.
It rose 4 percentage points, a 33% increase.
It rose 4 percentage points, a 50% increase.
It rose 50 percentage points, a 4% increase.

why.A: This treats the difference in points as the percent increase. A percent increase compares the change to the starting value, 8.
why.B: This divides the change by the new rate, 4/12, instead of the starting rate.
why.C: Correct — the rates differ by 12 − 8 = 4 percentage points, and that rise is 4/8 = 50% of the starting rate.
why.D: This swaps the two measures. The rates themselves differ by only 4 points.

context: A coat is marked 30% off, and a coupon takes an extra 20% off the sale price. The two discounts together equal a single discount of what percent?

why.A: This adds the two discounts. The 20% comes off the already-reduced price, so it takes off less than 20% of the original.
why.B: This is the fraction of the original price the buyer still pays, not the discount.
why.C: This multiplies the two discount rates, 0.3 × 0.2, instead of the fractions of the price that remain.
why.D: Correct — the buyer pays 70% and then 80% of that: 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the original, which is 44% off.

context: At an animal shelter, the ratio of cats to dogs is 4 : 5. After 6 more cats arrive and no other animals come or go, the numbers of cats and dogs are equal. How many dogs are at the shelter?

why.A: Correct — write the counts as 4k cats and 5k dogs. Then 4k + 6 = 5k gives k = 6, so there are 5 × 6 = 30 dogs.
why.B: This is the number of cats before the new ones arrived, 4 × 6.
why.C: This is the multiplier k, not the number of dogs.
why.D: This is the total number of animals before the new cats arrived, 24 + 30.

context: A 10-liter jug of juice that is 30% orange juice is poured together with 15 liters of juice that is 60% orange juice. What percent of the mixture is orange juice?

why.A: This averages 30% and 60% as if the amounts were equal. The larger 60% batch pulls the mixture above the midpoint.
why.B: Correct — the orange juice totals 0.3(10) + 0.6(15) = 3 + 9 = 12 liters out of 25 liters, and 12/25 = 48%.
why.C: This adds the two percents. Mixing cannot raise the concentration above the stronger batch.
why.D: This is the number of liters of orange juice, 12, not its share of the 25 liters.

context: A club’s yearly fee rose 10% last year and 10% again this year, and it is now $605. What was the fee two years ago?

why.A: This divides by 1.2, treating two 10% raises as one 20% raise. The second raise also applies to the first raise.
why.B: This takes 20% off $605. A decrease of 20% from the new fee does not undo an increase that was figured on the old fee.
why.C: Correct — two 10% increases multiply the fee by 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, so the earlier fee was 605 ÷ 1.21 = $500.
why.D: This takes 10% off twice. Each percent was figured on the smaller, earlier fee, so undoing it means dividing by 1.1, not multiplying by 0.9.

context: Ana’s salary is 20% more than Ben’s, and Ben’s salary is 20% less than Cal’s. Ana’s salary is what percent of Cal’s?

why.A: This assumes a 20% increase and a 20% decrease cancel. They are percents of different salaries.
why.B: This compares Ana with Ben only and ignores the step from Ben to Cal.
why.C: This compares Ben with Cal only and ignores Ana’s 20% more.
why.D: Correct — Ana earns 1.2 times Ben’s pay and Ben earns 0.8 times Cal’s, so Ana earns 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 times Cal’s.

context: In a recipe, the ratio of flour to sugar is 3 : 4, and the ratio of sugar to butter is 6 : 5. The recipe uses 10 cups of butter. How many cups of flour does it use?

why.A: Correct — make the sugar parts match: 3 : 4 = 9 : 12 and 6 : 5 = 12 : 10, so flour : sugar : butter = 9 : 12 : 10, and 10 cups of butter go with 9 cups of flour.
why.B: This joins the outer numbers directly as flour : butter = 3 : 5, treating 4 parts of sugar and 6 parts of sugar as the same amount.
why.C: This is the amount of sugar that goes with 10 cups of butter, not the amount of flour.
why.D: This cross-multiplies the wrong pair, making flour : butter = 3 × 5 : 4 × 6 = 15 : 24.

context: The positive number x is 150% of the number y. The number y is what percent of x + y?

why.A: This is x’s share of the total, 1.5y/(2.5y), not y’s.
why.B: Correct — x = 1.5y, so x + y = 2.5y, and y/(2.5y) = 0.4 = 40%.
why.C: This is y as a percent of x alone, 1/1.5. The question asks about the total x + y.
why.D: This is the total as a percent of y, the ratio turned upside down.

context: A table pairs the x-values 0, 1, 2 and 3 with the y-values 7, 10, 13 and 16. Which linear equation fits every pair in the table?

why.A: This swaps the slope and the intercept. At x = 1 it gives 10 but at x = 2 it gives 17, not 13.
why.B: This takes the y-value at x = 1 as the intercept. The intercept is the y-value at x = 0.
why.C: Correct — each step of 1 in x adds 3 to y, so the slope is 3, and y = 7 when x = 0.
why.D: This counts back one extra step, as if the first row were x = 1.

context: The water level w, in inches, in a draining tank t minutes after a valve opens is w = 60 − 2.5t. What does the 2.5 tell you?

choices.text: The water level rises 2.5 inches each minute.
The water level starts at 2.5 inches.
The tank is empty after 2.5 minutes.
The water level drops 2.5 inches each minute.

why.A: This misses the minus sign. The term is subtracted from 60, so w falls as t grows.
why.B: The starting level is the value at t = 0, which is 60 inches.
why.C: The tank is empty when 60 − 2.5t = 0, at t = 24 minutes.
why.D: Correct — 2.5 multiplies t, so every added minute lowers w by 2.5 inches.

context: Where does the graph of 3x + 5y = 30 cross the x-axis?

why.A: Correct — on the x-axis y = 0, so 3x = 30 and x = 10.
why.B: This is where the line crosses the y-axis, found by setting x = 0.
why.C: This divides 30 by the y-coefficient, 5, instead of the x-coefficient.
why.D: This finds 10 correctly but places it on the y-axis.

context: If ax + b = cx + d and a ≠ c, which expression is equal to x?

why.A: This moves b to the right side without changing its sign.
why.B: Correct — subtract cx and b from both sides to get ax − cx = d − b, so x(a − c) = d − b.
why.C: This adds b to the right side. Moving b across the equals sign subtracts it.
why.D: This adds cx to the left side instead of subtracting it.

context: A line has the equation y − 4 = −2(x + 3). Which equation describes the same line in slope-intercept form?

why.A: This distributes −2 to the 3 as +6 instead of −6.
why.B: This multiplies only the x by −2 and leaves the +3 alone, so y − 4 = −2x + 3.
why.C: Correct — distribute to get y − 4 = −2x − 6, then add 4 to both sides.
why.D: This subtracts 4 from the right side instead of adding it when isolating y.

context: A line has a negative slope and a positive y-intercept. Which quadrant of the coordinate plane does the line NOT pass through?

why.A: Just right of the positive y-intercept, the line is still above the x-axis, which is Quadrant I.
why.B: To the left of the y-axis, the line rises above its positive intercept, which is Quadrant II.
why.C: Past its x-intercept the falling line drops below the x-axis on the right, which is Quadrant IV.
why.D: Correct — the line crosses the positive y-axis and falls to the right into Quadrant IV. To the left of the y-axis it rises, staying in Quadrant II, so it never reaches Quadrant III.

context: If 3x − 2y = 8, what is the value of 6y − 9x?

why.B: This factors out 3 but misses that 6y − 9x runs in the opposite order from 3x − 2y, which flips the sign.
why.C: This sees the order is reversed but leaves out the factor of 3.
why.D: This multiplies by −2, matching the 2y term but not the 3x term.

context: The graph of ax + 3y = 12 crosses the x-axis at a point 4 units farther from the origin than where it crosses the y-axis. Both intercepts are positive. What is the value of a?

why.A: This sets the x-intercept equal to 4, the y-intercept itself, instead of 4 more than it.
why.B: Correct — the y-intercept is 12/3 = 4, so the x-intercept is 8. Then a(8) = 12 gives a = 3/2.
why.C: This takes 12 as the y-intercept, so the x-intercept becomes 16. Setting x = 0 leaves 3y = 12, so y = 4.
why.D: This finds the x-intercept, 8, but then divides 8 by 12 instead of 12 by 8.

context: Which of the following equations has no solution?

why.A: Both sides are the same expression, so every x works: infinitely many solutions, the opposite of none.
why.B: The x-terms have different coefficients, 3 and −3, so there is exactly one solution, x = 2.
why.C: Correct — the left side is 3x − 6, and 3x − 6 = 3x + 6 would need −6 = 6, which is never true.
why.D: The x-terms have different coefficients, so there is exactly one solution, x = 0.

context: Car A is at mile marker 20 and drives toward higher markers at 55 miles per hour. At the same moment, car B is at mile marker 200 and drives toward lower markers on the same road at 65 miles per hour. At what mile marker do the cars meet?

why.A: This is halfway between the markers. The faster car B covers more than half the gap.
why.B: This subtracts car A’s distance, 82.5, from marker 200. Car B’s own distance is 65 × 1.5 = 97.5.
why.C: This is the distance car B travels, not the marker where the cars meet.
why.D: Correct — the gap of 180 miles closes at 55 + 65 = 120 miles per hour, taking 1.5 hours. Car A covers 55 × 1.5 = 82.5 miles, reaching marker 102.5.

context: A tank drains at a constant rate. Two minutes after draining begins it holds 58 liters, and five minutes after draining begins it holds 43 liters. How many minutes after draining begins will the tank be empty?

why.A: Correct — the tank loses (58 − 43)/3 = 5 liters per minute, so it started with 58 + 2(5) = 68 liters and is empty after 68 ÷ 5 = 13.6 minutes.
why.B: This is 58 ÷ 5, the time to drain after the 2-minute reading. It must be added to those first 2 minutes.
why.C: This is 43 ÷ 5, the time left after the 5-minute reading, not the time from the start.
why.D: This adds 5 minutes to 58 ÷ 5, pairing the 58-liter reading with the wrong time.

context: A and B are 2 × 2 matrices. Which statement about the products AB and BA is true?

choices.text: AB and BA are always equal.
AB and BA are not always equal.
AB is found by multiplying the matching entries of A and B.
AB is defined only when A and B are the same matrix.

why.A: This carries over the rule for multiplying numbers. Matrix products usually change when the order changes.
why.B: Correct — matrix multiplication depends on order. For example, [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and [[1, 0], [1, 1]] give different products in the two orders.
why.C: Matrix products combine a row of the first matrix with a column of the second, not matching entries.
why.D: Two 2 × 2 matrices can always be multiplied, in either order.

why.A: This adds 6 and −4 without dividing by 2, finding 2a + 2b rather than a + b.
why.B: This multiplies each output by 2 instead of dividing, getting 12 and −8.

why.D: This drops the sign of b, adding 3 and 2.

why.B: This puts the two columns in the wrong order.
why.C: This keeps only the entries on the main diagonal.

context: Which of the following matrices does NOT have a multiplicative inverse?

why.A: Correct — its determinant is 6(6) − 4(9) = 0, and a matrix with determinant 0 has no inverse.
why.B: Zero entries do not prevent an inverse. The determinant is 0 − 36 = −36.
why.C: A negative entry does not prevent an inverse. The determinant is 36 + 36 = 72.
why.D: Being symmetric does not prevent an inverse. The determinant is 4 − 9 = −5.

context: The augmented matrix [[1, 2 | 5], [0, 1 | 2]] represents a system of equations in x and y. What is the value of x?

why.A: This reads the top-right number as x, ignoring the 2y in row 1.
why.B: Correct — row 2 says y = 2, and row 1 says x + 2y = 5, so x = 5 − 4 = 1.
why.C: This is the value of y from row 2.
why.D: This adds 2y instead of subtracting it when solving x + 2y = 5.

context: What is the entry in row 2, column 1 of the product [[1, 3], [2, −1]] · [[4, 0], [5, 2]]?

why.A: This multiplies the row 2, column 1 entries of the two matrices, 2 × 5, as if products went entry by entry.
why.B: This drops the sign of −1, finding 2(4) + 1(5).
why.C: Correct — row 2 of the first matrix times column 1 of the second is 2(4) + (−1)(5) = 3.
why.D: This uses row 1 instead of row 2: 1(4) + 3(5) = 19.

context: Matrix A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] has zeros everywhere off its main diagonal. Which matrix is A⁴?

why.A: This multiplies each entry by 4 instead of raising it to the 4th power.
why.B: This is A², which is only halfway to A⁴.
why.C: This adds 4 to each diagonal entry.
why.D: Correct — for a matrix with zeros off the main diagonal, each power just raises the diagonal entries: 2⁴ = 16 and 3⁴ = 81.

context: Expanding along the first row, find the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix [[1, 2, 0], [3, −1, 2], [0, 4, 1]].

why.B: This adds the middle term instead of subtracting it. The signs along a row alternate +, −, +.
why.C: This stops after the first term of the expansion.
why.D: This multiplies the main diagonal, 1 · (−1) · 1, a shortcut that works only when every entry below the diagonal is 0.

context: Matrix A = [[a, 2], [3, b]] satisfies A · [[1], [2]] = [[7], [11]]. What is the determinant of A?

why.A: This adds the two diagonal products, 12 + 6, instead of subtracting.
why.B: Correct — a + 4 = 7 gives a = 3, and 3 + 2b = 11 gives b = 4. The determinant is 3(4) − 2(3) = 6.
why.C: This stops at the main-diagonal product ab.
why.D: This subtracts in the wrong order, 2(3) − 3(4).

context: For which value of a does B = [[a, 1], [0, −1]] satisfy B² = I, where I is the 2 × 2 identity matrix?

why.A: This makes a² = 1, but the top-right entry a − 1 is then −2, not 0.
why.B: This makes the top-left entry a² = 0, not 1.
why.C: Correct — B² = [[a², a − 1], [0, 1]]. This equals I only when a² = 1 and a − 1 = 0, so a = 1.
why.D: This sets a − 1 = 1, reading the top-right entry of I as 1. That entry is 0.

context: The determinant of a 3 × 3 matrix A is 4. If every entry of A is doubled, what is the determinant of the new matrix?

why.A: This doubles the determinant once, as if only one row were scaled.
why.B: This uses 2² × 4, the rule for a 2 × 2 matrix.
why.C: This multiplies 4 by 2 × 3, using the size of the matrix as a factor.
why.D: Correct — multiplying a 3 × 3 matrix by 2 doubles each of its 3 rows, and each row multiplies the determinant by 2, so det(2A) = 2³ × 4.

context: What is the value of |−6i|?

why.A: Correct — −6i is the point (0, −6) in the complex plane, which is 6 units from 0.
why.B: This keeps the sign. An absolute value is a distance, so it is never negative.
why.C: This squares the 6 and forgets the square root in |a + bi| = √(a² + b²).
why.D: This drops the sign but keeps the i. The absolute value is a real number.

context: What is the real part of (3 − 2i) · i?

why.A: This is the real part before multiplying by i.
why.B: Correct — (3 − 2i)i = 3i − 2i² = 3i + 2, so the real part is 2.
why.C: This treats i² as 1, so −2i² stays −2.
why.D: This assumes multiplying by i always leaves a purely imaginary number.

context: What is the value of √(−4) · √(−9)?

why.A: This combines them as √((−4)(−9)) = √36. That rule holds only when the numbers under the roots are not both negative.
why.B: This multiplies 2i by 3i and replaces i² with −1 but leaves an extra i behind.
why.C: Correct — √(−4) = 2i and √(−9) = 3i, so the product is 6i² = −6.
why.D: This adds 2i and 3i instead of multiplying.

context: A complex number z satisfies z + 2z̄ = 9 − 4i, where z̄ is the conjugate of z. What is z?

why.A: This matches −bi to −4i but keeps the sign when writing z. Since −b = −4, b is 4.
why.B: This treats z̄ as z, solving 3z = 9 − 4i.
why.C: This takes the conjugate of the right side instead of solving for z.
why.D: Correct — with z = a + bi, z + 2z̄ = (a + bi) + 2(a − bi) = 3a − bi. So 3a = 9 and −b = −4, giving a = 3 and b = 4.

context: In the complex plane, the numbers z with |z − (2 + i)| = 5 form a circle. What number is at the center of the circle?

why.A: Correct — |z − w| is the distance from z to w, so these are the points 5 units from 2 + i.
why.B: This flips the signs, as if the equation described distance from −(2 + i).
why.C: This is the radius of the circle, not its center.
why.D: This takes the origin as the center, which would need |z| = 5.

context: What is (2i)³?

why.A: This takes i³ as i. Since i² = −1, i³ = −i.
why.B: Correct — (2i)³ = 2³ · i³ = 8 · (−i) = −8i.
why.C: This takes i³ as −1, which is the value of i².
why.D: This multiplies 2 by 3 instead of cubing it.

context: If z = 2 + i, what is the value of z² − 4z?

why.A: This adds 4i instead of subtracting it when taking away 4z.
why.B: This takes i² as +1, so z² = 5 + 4i, and then subtracts 8 + 4i.
why.C: Correct — z² = 4 + 4i + i² = 3 + 4i, and 4z = 8 + 4i, so z² − 4z = −5.
why.D: This is z² alone. The 4z still has to be subtracted.

context: In the complex plane, the points 0, z = 3 + i and iz are the vertices of a triangle. What is the area of the triangle?

why.A: This multiplies the two perpendicular sides but forgets the 1/2.
why.B: This is the length of each of the two equal sides, not the area.
why.C: This computes (1/2)|3 · 3 − 1 · (−1)| but drops the sign, finding (1/2)(9 − 1).
why.D: Correct — iz = −1 + 3i. Multiplying by i turns z a quarter turn, so the sides from 0 to z and to iz are perpendicular and each has length √10. The area is (1/2)(√10)(√10) = 5.

context: What is the value of i + 2i² + 3i³ + 4i⁴?

why.A: Correct — the terms are i, −2, −3i and 4, which add to (−2 + 4) + (1 − 3)i = 2 − 2i.
why.B: This treats every power of i as 1.
why.C: This takes i³ as i instead of −i.
why.D: This takes i⁴ as −1 instead of 1.

context: What is the smallest positive integer n for which (1 + i)ⁿ is a positive real number?

why.A: This gives −4, which is real but negative.
why.B: Correct — (1 + i)² = 2i, so (1 + i)⁴ = (2i)² = −4 and (1 + i)⁸ = (−4)² = 16, the first positive real power.
why.C: This gives 2i, which is purely imaginary.
why.D: This gives 1 + i itself, which has an imaginary part.

context: The quotient (a − i)/(1 + i), where a is a real number, has a real part of 0 and an imaginary part that is not 0. What is the value of a?

why.A: This makes the imaginary part 0, so the quotient is the real number −1.
why.B: This assumes −i/(1 + i) is purely imaginary. It equals (−1 − i)/2, which has a real part.

context: A florist has 48 roses and 36 lilies. She wants to make identical bouquets that use every flower, with each bouquet holding the same number of roses and the same number of lilies. What is the greatest number of bouquets she can make?

why.A: This is the least common multiple of 48 and 36. Splitting flowers into groups calls for a common factor, not a common multiple.
why.B: Correct — the number of bouquets must divide both 48 and 36, and the greatest such number is their greatest common factor, 12.
why.C: Six bouquets would work, but 6 is not the greatest number that divides both 48 and 36.
why.D: This is the total number of flowers, which would put one flower in each bouquet and make them unequal.

context: What is the value of (8 − 2 × 3)/(4 − 2)²?

why.A: This works the numerator left to right, (8 − 2) × 3 = 18. Multiplication comes before subtraction.
why.B: This leaves out the square in the denominator, giving 2/2.
why.C: Correct — the numerator is 8 − 6 = 2, the denominator is 2² = 4, and 2/4 = 1/2.
why.D: This squares each term in the denominator separately, 16 − 4 = 12, instead of squaring the difference.

context: The three-digit number 4d6 has tens digit d and is divisible by 9. What is the value of d?

why.A: This makes the digits add to 15, which is divisible by 3 but not by 9.
why.B: This uses the divisor itself as the digit. Then the digits add to 19, which is not a multiple of 9.
why.C: This makes the digits add to 10, which is not a multiple of 9.
why.D: Correct — a number is divisible by 9 when its digits add to a multiple of 9. Here 4 + d + 6 = 10 + d, which is 18 when d = 8.

context: What is the units digit of 3²³?

why.A: Correct — the units digits of the powers of 3 repeat 3, 9, 7, 1. Since 23 = 4 × 5 + 3, 3²³ ends like 3³, in 7.
why.B: This takes the remainder, 3, as the units digit itself instead of as a position in the cycle 3, 9, 7, 1.

why.D: This lands one position early in the cycle, on the units digit of 3².

context: Which fraction is equal to the repeating decimal 0.272727…, in which the digits 27 repeat forever?

why.A: This stops the decimal after two places, 0.27, which leaves off every later 27.
why.B: Correct — two repeating digits go over 99: 27/99, which reduces to 3/11.
why.C: This puts 27 over 90, a rule for a decimal in which only one digit repeats after one digit that does not.

context: Two positive integers have a greatest common factor of 6 and a least common multiple of 72. One of the integers is 18. What is the other?

why.A: This divides the LCM by the GCF. The other number must also have 18 as a partner in the product.
why.B: This divides the LCM by 18. Then GCF(18, 4) = 2, not 6.
why.C: Correct — for two positive integers, GCF × LCM equals their product, so the other integer is (6 × 72)/18 = 24. Check: GCF(18, 24) = 6 and LCM(18, 24) = 72.
why.D: This is the product of the GCF and the LCM, which equals the product of both numbers, not the other number alone.

context: The numbers x and y satisfy x < 0 < y. Which of the following must be positive?

why.A: The sign depends on which number is farther from 0. With x = −5 and y = 2, x + y is negative.
why.B: A negative times a positive is negative.
why.C: This is a negative number minus a positive one, which is always negative.
why.D: Correct — subtracting a negative x adds its size, so y − x is a positive number plus a positive number.

context: The number 25! is the product of all the integers from 1 through 25. How many zeros are at the end of 25! when it is written out in full?

why.A: Correct — each end zero needs a factor of 10 = 2 × 5, and factors of 2 are plentiful. The factors of 5 come from 5, 10, 15 and 20 (one each) and 25 (two), for 6 in all.
why.B: This counts the five multiples of 5 once each and misses that 25 = 5 × 5 supplies a second factor of 5.
why.C: This counts only the multiples of 10, which are not the only sources of a 5 and a 2.
why.D: This counts the multiples of 5 and then counts 10 and 20 a second time. Each of them holds just one 5.

context: How many of the integers from 1 through 100 are perfect squares or perfect cubes?

why.A: This adds the squares and the cubes without removing 1 and 64, which were counted in both lists.
why.B: Correct — there are 10 squares (1 through 100) and 4 cubes (1, 8, 27, 64). The numbers 1 and 64 are both, so they are counted once: 10 + 4 − 2 = 12.
why.C: This removes only one of the numbers that is both a square and a cube. Both 1 = 1² = 1³ and 64 = 8² = 4³ repeat.
why.D: This counts only the perfect squares.

context: The number p is a prime greater than 3. What is the remainder when p² is divided by 12?

why.A: Trying a few primes, 5, 7, 11, 13, gives 25, 49, 121, 169, and each leaves a remainder of 1. The remainder never changes.
why.B: This tries p = 3, which the question rules out. 3² = 9 leaves remainder 9.
why.C: Correct — a prime greater than 3 is one more or one less than a multiple of 6, so p = 6k ± 1 and p² = 36k² ± 12k + 1, which is 1 more than a multiple of 12.
why.D: This tries p = 2, which the question rules out. 2² = 4 leaves remainder 4.

context: The positive integers x and y satisfy x² − y² = 17. What is the value of x + y?

why.A: This is x − y, the smaller of the two factors of 17.
why.B: This is x alone.
why.C: This is y alone.
why.D: Correct — x² − y² = (x − y)(x + y) = 17. Since 17 is prime and x + y is the larger factor, x + y = 17 and x − y = 1, giving x = 9 and y = 8.

context: What is the value of 5⁰ + 5⁻¹?

why.A: Correct — 5⁰ = 1 and 5⁻¹ = 1/5, so the sum is 1 + 1/5 = 6/5.
why.B: This takes 5⁰ as 0. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1.
why.C: This reads 5⁻¹ as −5. A negative exponent means a reciprocal, not a negative number.
why.D: This takes 5⁰ as 5, as if the zero exponent left the base unchanged.

context: What is ∛54 in simplest radical form?

why.A: This follows the square-root pattern, 54 = 9 × 6, and ignores that the root is a cube root.

why.D: This subtracts the leading numbers, 8.4 − 2.1, instead of dividing them.

context: What is the value of (4/9)^(−3/2)?

why.A: This drops the negative sign of the exponent, so the fraction is never flipped.
why.B: This reads the negative exponent as making the value negative. A negative exponent takes a reciprocal.
why.C: This flips and cubes, (9/4)³, but leaves out the square root that the 2 in the denominator calls for.
why.D: Correct — the negative exponent flips the fraction to 9/4, the square root gives 3/2, and cubing gives 27/8.

context: Which of the following is equal to 2⁵ + 2⁵ + 2⁵ + 2⁵?

why.A: Correct — four copies of 2⁵ is 4 · 2⁵ = 2² · 2⁵ = 2⁷.
why.B: This multiplies the exponent by 4. That would be 2⁵ multiplied by itself four times, not added four times.
why.C: This adds the bases, 2 + 2 + 2 + 2, and keeps the exponent.
why.D: This adds the number of terms, 4, to the exponent. Writing 4 as 2² adds 2, not 4.

context: If x^(2/3) = 9 and x > 0, what is the value of x?

why.A: This multiplies 9 by 2/3. Undoing an exponent takes the reciprocal power, not a product.
why.B: Correct — raise both sides to the 3/2 power: x = 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27.

context: What is the value of (−8)^(2/3)?

why.A: This finds ∛(−8) = −2 and then squares only the 2, keeping the minus sign outside the square.
why.B: This multiplies −8 by the exponent 2/3 instead of raising −8 to that power.
why.C: Correct — take the cube root first: ∛(−8) = −2, and then (−2)² = 4.
why.D: This squares −8 to get 64 and then takes the square root instead of the cube root.

context: Four numbers are written as roots: √2, ∛3, ⁴√5 and ⁶√10. Which of them has the greatest value?

why.A: This picks the largest number under a radical. A sixth root shrinks 10 more than a fourth root shrinks 5.
why.B: This picks the smallest index, as if a square root always gives the larger result. √2 ≈ 1.41 is the least of the four.
why.C: This compares only √2 and ∛3. It beats √2, but ⁴√5 ≈ 1.50 is larger still.
why.D: Correct — raise each to the 12th power: (√2)¹² = 64, (∛3)¹² = 81, (⁴√5)¹² = 125 and (⁶√10)¹² = 100. The largest is ⁴√5.

context: The number a satisfies √(7 + 4√3) = a + √3. What is the value of a?

why.A: Correct — (a + √3)² = a² + 3 + 2a√3. Matching 7 + 4√3 gives 2a = 4, so a = 2, and a² + 3 = 7 checks.
why.B: This reads a off the coefficient 4 of √3. That coefficient is 2a, not a.
why.C: This takes the square root of each term under the radical separately. The root of a sum does not split that way.
why.D: This satisfies a² + 3 = 7 but not 2a = 4, and −2 + √3 is negative, so it cannot equal a square root.

context: The time a planet takes to orbit its star is proportional to d^(3/2), where d is the planet’s average distance from the star. If one planet is 4 times as far from the star as another, how many times as long is its orbit?

why.A: This multiplies 4 by 3/2 instead of raising 4 to the 3/2 power.
why.B: Correct — the ratio of the times is 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8.
why.C: This cubes 4 and leaves out the square root.
why.D: This takes the square root of 4 and leaves out the cube.

context: What is the value of 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 4⁴⁹?

why.A: This subtracts the exponents, 100 − 49, while the bases are still different.
why.B: This rewrites 4⁴⁹ as 2⁹⁹, adding 1 to the exponent instead of doubling it.
why.C: Correct — 4⁴⁹ = (2²)⁴⁹ = 2⁹⁸, so the quotient is 2¹⁰⁰⁻⁹⁸ = 2² = 4.
why.D: This divides in the wrong order, 4⁴⁹ ÷ 2¹⁰⁰.

context: A scatterplot shows the outdoor temperature and the heating bill for a house over 30 months. As the temperature rises, the bill falls, and the points lie close to a straight line. Which phrase best describes the relationship?

why.A: A positive correlation means both quantities rise together. Here the bill falls as the temperature rises.
why.B: The direction is right, but points lying close to a line show a strong relationship, not a weak one.
why.C: The points follow a clear downward line, so the two quantities are related.
why.D: Correct — one quantity falls as the other rises, which is negative, and points lying close to a line make it strong.

context: Maya’s score on a statewide exam is at the 80th percentile. Which statement must be true?

choices.text: About 80% of the students who took the exam scored at or below Maya.
Maya answered about 80% of the exam questions correctly.
About 80% of the students who took the exam scored above Maya.
Maya’s score was 80 points above the mean score of the exam.

why.A: Correct — a percentile ranks a score against everyone else’s. The 80th percentile sits at or above 80% of the scores.
why.B: This confuses a percentile with a percent correct. A percentile compares Maya with other students, not with the exam.
why.C: This reverses the ranking. At the 80th percentile, only about 20% scored higher.
why.D: A percentile says nothing about points above the mean, only about the share of scores below.

context: A poll estimates that 54% of a town’s voters support a new library, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which interval gives the plausible values for the true percent of supporters?

why.A: This splits the margin in half across the two sides. The full 3 points go in each direction.
why.B: Correct — a margin of error extends the same distance on both sides of the estimate: 54 − 3 to 54 + 3.
why.C: This applies the margin only below the estimate.
why.D: This applies the margin only above the estimate.

context: At a company, 60% of the employees are in Division A, where the mean salary is $40,000. The rest are in Division B, where the mean salary is $55,000. What is the mean salary of all the employees?

why.A: This averages the two means as if the divisions were the same size. Division A is larger, so the overall mean sits closer to $40,000.
why.B: This swaps the weights, giving Division B the 60% share.
why.C: Correct — weight each mean by its share of the employees: 0.6(40,000) + 0.4(55,000) = 24,000 + 22,000.
why.D: This adds the two means instead of averaging them.

context: A data set has a first quartile of 20 and a third quartile of 32. A common rule calls a value an outlier if it is more than 1.5 times the interquartile range above the third quartile. Above what value is a data point an outlier by this rule?

why.A: This adds the interquartile range itself, 12, and leaves out the factor of 1.5.
why.B: This adds half the interquartile range, 6, instead of one and a half times it.
why.C: This is the lower cutoff, 20 − 18, which marks outliers at the bottom of the data.
why.D: Correct — the interquartile range is 32 − 20 = 12, and 1.5 × 12 = 18, so the cutoff is 32 + 18 = 50.

context: Daily high temperatures for a month have a standard deviation of 5 degrees Celsius. Each temperature is converted to degrees Fahrenheit with F = 1.8C + 32. What is the standard deviation of the converted temperatures, in degrees Fahrenheit?

why.A: Correct — multiplying every value by 1.8 multiplies the spread by 1.8, and adding 32 shifts every value equally without changing the spread: 1.8 × 5 = 9.
why.B: This applies the whole conversion, 1.8(5) + 32. Adding 32 moves every temperature up by the same amount, so it leaves the spread alone.
why.C: This assumes the spread does not change. The factor of 1.8 stretches the distances between values.
why.D: This adds 32 to the spread and leaves out the factor of 1.8. Adding 32 shifts every temperature equally, so only the 1.8 matters.

context: Two box plots summarize the scores of two classes. Class A: first quartile 50, median 60, third quartile 70. Class B: first quartile 61, median 65, third quartile 69. Which statement is supported by the box plots?

choices.text: Class A has the higher median and the smaller interquartile range.
Class B has the higher median and the smaller interquartile range.
Class B has the higher median and the larger interquartile range.
Class A has the higher median and the larger interquartile range.

why.A: A’s median, 60, is the lower one, and its middle half spans 20 points against B’s 8.
why.B: Correct — B’s median, 65, beats A’s 60, and B’s interquartile range, 69 − 61 = 8, is smaller than A’s 70 − 50 = 20.
why.C: The median is right, but B’s middle half spans only 8 points, the narrower of the two.
why.D: A’s interquartile range is the larger, but its median, 60, is below B’s 65.

context: A data set contains 11 different numbers. Each of the 5 numbers below the median is decreased by 5, and the other numbers do not change. Which of the following is certain to stay the same?

why.A: Five values each drop by 5, so the total drops by 25 and the mean drops by 25/11.
why.B: The smallest value drops by 5 while the largest does not change, so the range grows by 5.
why.C: Correct — the middle value is untouched, and the lowered values were already below it, so it is still the sixth of the eleven values in order.
why.D: The first quartile lies below the median, so it drops by 5 while the third quartile stays put, widening the interquartile range.

context: The mean of 12 numbers is 40. After two of the numbers are removed, the mean of the remaining numbers is 38. What is the mean of the two numbers that were removed?

why.A: This is the sum of the two removed numbers, not their mean.
why.B: This averages the two means, 40 and 38, which describe groups of different sizes.
why.C: This assumes the removed numbers sit as far above 40 as the new mean sits below it. The two removed numbers carry the weight of ten others.
why.D: Correct — the 12 numbers total 480 and the remaining 10 total 380, so the two removed numbers total 100, a mean of 50.

context: The mean of a data set is 20. When the value 50 is added to the set, the mean rises to 22. How many values were in the set before 50 was added?

why.A: Correct — with n values, 20n + 50 = 22(n + 1), so 2n = 28 and n = 14.
why.B: This is (50 − 20)/(22 − 20), which counts the values after 50 joins the set, not before.
why.C: This is 2n, found correctly, but not divided by 2.
why.D: This divides the new value by the rise in the mean, 50/2, leaving out the old mean entirely.

context: A data set has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 6. A new value of 50 is added to the set. Which statement describes the effect on the mean and the standard deviation?

choices.text: The mean stays the same and the standard deviation stays the same.
The mean stays the same and the standard deviation decreases.
The mean stays the same and the standard deviation increases.
The mean increases and the standard deviation stays the same.

why.A: A value at the mean adds no spread, but the other deviations are now shared across one more value, so the standard deviation shrinks.
why.B: Correct — a value equal to the mean leaves the mean unchanged. It adds a deviation of 0 while the count grows, so the typical distance from the mean shrinks.
why.C: Adding a value adds spread only when it lies away from the mean. This one lies exactly on it.
why.D: Adding a value equal to the mean cannot move the mean.

context: The odds against a team winning its next game are 7 : 3. What is the probability that the team wins?

why.A: This writes the odds as a fraction. Odds compare wins with losses, while a probability compares wins with all outcomes.
why.B: This is the probability that the team loses.
why.C: Correct — odds of 7 : 3 against mean 7 losing outcomes for every 3 winning ones out of 10 in all, so the chance of a win is 3/10.
why.D: This is the odds against written as a fraction, and it is greater than 1, which no probability can be.

context: A basketball player makes 80% of her free throws. If she takes 25 free throws, how many should she be expected to make?

why.A: This is the expected number of misses, 20% of 25.
why.B: This divides 25 by 0.8. That gives more makes than tries.
why.C: This takes the percent as a count, ignoring that there are only 25 tries.
why.D: Correct — the expected number is the probability times the number of tries: 0.8 × 25 = 20.

context: Each spin of a spinner lands on exactly one color. The probability of red is 0.35 and the probability of blue is 0.25. What is the probability that a spin lands on red or blue?

why.A: Correct — a spin cannot be both red and blue, so the probabilities add: 0.35 + 0.25 = 0.6.
why.B: This multiplies the probabilities, which gives the chance of red and blue on two separate spins, not red or blue on one.
why.C: This subtracts the smaller probability from the larger.
why.D: This is the probability that a spin lands on neither red nor blue.

context: A point is chosen at random on the number line between 0 and 10. What is the probability that the point is within 2 units of 7?

why.A: This counts only the 2 units on one side of 7. The points from 5 to 7 and from 7 to 9 both qualify.
why.B: Correct — the points within 2 units of 7 run from 5 to 9, a length of 4 out of 10.
why.C: This is the chance of landing below 7, which ignores the distance of 2.
why.D: This measures from 7 to the end of the line, 3 units, instead of the 4 units from 5 to 9.

context: Five different books are placed in a row on a shelf. Two particular books must be at the two ends of the row. How many different arrangements are possible?

why.A: This fixes which book goes on the left end. The two end books can also trade places.
why.B: This is 5!, every arrangement with no restriction.
why.C: Correct — the two end books can be placed in 2 ways, and the other 3 books fill the middle in 3! = 6 ways: 2 × 6 = 12.
why.D: This glues the two books together side by side, 4! × 2, instead of placing them at opposite ends.

context: A spinner lands on red with probability 1/4. It is spun 3 times. What is the probability that it lands on red exactly once?

why.A: This is the chance of one particular order, such as red first. The red could come on any of the 3 spins.
why.B: This is the chance of at least one red, 1 − (3/4)³, which also counts two or three reds.
why.C: This multiplies 1/4 by the 3 spins and ignores that the other spins must miss red.
why.D: Correct — one red and two non-reds has probability (1/4)(3/4)² = 9/64, and the red can come on any of the 3 spins: 3 × 9/64.

context: The probability that a bus is late is 0.2 and the probability that it rains is 0.3. The two events are independent. What is the probability that the bus is not late and it does not rain?

why.A: Correct — the complements are 0.8 and 0.7, and independent events multiply: 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.56.
why.B: This subtracts both probabilities from 1, as if lateness and rain could never happen together.
why.C: This is the probability that both events happen, 0.2 × 0.3.
why.D: This is the probability that at least one of the events happens, 1 − 0.56.

context: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the larger of the two numbers rolled is 4? (If both dice show the same number, that number counts as the larger.)

why.A: This is the chance that at least one die shows 4, which includes rolls like (4, 6) whose larger number is 6.
why.B: Correct — both dice at most 4 happens in 4 × 4 = 16 ways, and both at most 3 in 9 ways. The larger number is exactly 4 in 16 − 9 = 7 ways.
why.C: This treats the larger number like a single die, equally likely to be any of 1 through 6. Larger values are more likely to be the maximum.
why.D: This is 9/36, the chance that both dice are at most 3.

context: A raffle sells 500 tickets at $2 each. One ticket wins $300 and two other tickets win $50 each. What is the expected net gain for a person who buys one ticket?

why.A: This is the expected prize and leaves out the $2 cost of the ticket.
why.B: This counts only one of the two $50 prizes.
why.C: Correct — the expected prize is (300 + 50 + 50)/500 = $0.80, and the ticket costs $2, so the expected net gain is 0.80 − 2.00.
why.D: This charges the $2 only to the losing tickets. Every ticket costs $2, including the three that win.

context: Three people are chosen at random, and each person’s birth month is equally likely to be any of the 12 months, independently of the others. What is the probability that all three were born in different months?

why.A: This is the probability that at least two of them share a month, the complement.
why.B: This checks only whether the second person differs from the first.
why.C: This is the probability that all three share one month.
why.D: Correct — the second person misses the first person’s month with probability 11/12, and the third misses both with probability 10/12: (11/12)(10/12) = 110/144.

context: How many 4-digit even numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 if no digit is used more than once?

why.A: Correct — fill the ones place first with one of the 3 even digits, then the other places in 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 ways: 3 × 60 = 180.
why.B: This is 6 × 5 × 4 × 3, every 4-digit arrangement, even or odd.
why.C: This fills the other three places but forgets that the ones digit itself has 3 choices.
why.D: This allows digits to repeat, 6 × 6 × 6 × 3.

context: Two triangles are known to share three measurements. Which of the following sets of matching measurements does NOT guarantee that the triangles are congruent?

choices.text: two sides and the angle between them
two sides and an angle not between them
two angles and the side between them
all three pairs of matching sides

why.A: This is side-angle-side, which fixes the triangle completely.
why.B: Correct — this is side-side-angle. The given side opposite the angle can swing to two different positions, so two different triangles can share these measurements.
why.C: This is angle-side-angle, which fixes the triangle completely.
why.D: This is side-side-side. Three side lengths allow only one triangle.

context: The straight arm of a crane is hinged at ground level and makes a 60° angle with the level ground. The tip of the arm is 12 meters above the ground. How long is the arm?

why.A: This treats the height as the shorter leg and doubles it. The height is opposite the 60° angle, so it is the longer leg.
why.B: This multiplies 12 by √3/2 instead of dividing by it, which makes the arm shorter than the height of its tip.
why.C: Correct — the arm is the hypotenuse of a 30°-60°-90° triangle, and the 12-meter height is the leg opposite 60°, the longer leg. The hypotenuse is 2/√3 times that leg: 24/√3 = 8√3.
why.D: This is the shorter leg, the ground distance from the hinge to the point under the tip.

context: In triangle PQR, PQ = 5, QR = 9 and PR = 7. Which angle of the triangle is smallest?

choices.text: a tie between P and Q

why.A: Angle P is opposite QR, the longest side, so it is the largest angle.
why.B: Angle Q is opposite PR, the middle side, so it is the middle angle.
why.C: Equal angles need equal opposite sides, and all three sides here differ.
why.D: Correct — the smallest angle lies opposite the shortest side. The shortest side is PQ, and the angle across from it is at R.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = 6, AC = 9 and BC = 10. Segment AD bisects angle A, with D on side BC. What is the length of BD?

why.A: Correct — an angle bisector splits the opposite side in the ratio of the two sides beside it: BD : DC = 6 : 9, so BD = (6/15)(10) = 4.
why.B: This puts D at the midpoint of BC. That is where a median lands, not an angle bisector, unless AB = AC.
why.C: This is DC, the part next to the longer side AC.
why.D: This divides 6 × 10 by 9 alone. The ratio is taken out of the total 6 + 9 = 15 parts.

context: One leg of a right triangle is twice as long as the other, and the hypotenuse has length 10. What is the length of the shorter leg?

why.A: This adds the legs, a + 2a = 10, as if the two legs together were as long as the hypotenuse.
why.B: Correct — with legs a and 2a, a² + 4a² = 100, so a² = 20 and a = 2√5.
why.C: This treats the longer leg, 2a, as the hypotenuse.
why.D: This is the longer leg, 2a.

context: In triangle ABC, AB = BC. Angle A measures (x + 25)° and angle C measures (2x − 5)°. What is the measure of angle B?

why.A: This is the measure of angle A or angle C, the equal base angles, not angle B.
why.B: This is the value of x, not an angle of the triangle.
why.C: Correct — the angles opposite the equal sides are equal, so x + 25 = 2x − 5 and x = 30. Each base angle is 55°, and angle B = 180° − 110° = 70°.
why.D: This subtracts only one base angle from 180°.

context: A regular hexagon has sides of length 6. What is the distance between two opposite sides of the hexagon?

why.A: This is the distance between two opposite vertices, which is two full sides.
why.B: This is one triangle’s height, the distance from the center to a side, only halfway across.
why.C: This uses a 45°-45°-90° ratio. The triangles inside a regular hexagon are equilateral.
why.D: Correct — the hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles of side 6. Opposite sides are two triangle heights apart, and each height is 3√3.

context: An equilateral triangle and a square have the same perimeter. What is the ratio of the area of the triangle to the area of the square?

why.A: Correct — if the square has side s, the triangle has side 4s/3. Its area is (√3/4)(16s²/9) = 4√3s²/9, and the square’s is s².
why.B: This gives the two figures the same side length. Equal perimeters make the triangle’s sides longer by a factor of 4/3.
why.C: This is the ratio of the side lengths, not of the areas.
why.D: This squares the side ratio but leaves out the √3/4 factor in the area of an equilateral triangle.

context: A 30°-60°-90° triangle has a hypotenuse of length 12. What is the length of the altitude drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse?

why.A: This is half the hypotenuse, the length of the median to the hypotenuse. The altitude is shorter than the median here.
why.B: Correct — the legs are 6 and 6√3. Two times the area equals leg times leg and also hypotenuse times altitude: 6 · 6√3 = 12h, so h = 3√3.
why.C: This is the longer leg, not the altitude.
why.D: This divides the area, 18√3, by the hypotenuse without first doubling the area.

context: Both legs of a right triangle are made 50% longer. By what percent does the hypotenuse increase?

why.A: This is the increase in the area, which scales by 1.5² = 2.25.
why.B: This adds a 50% increase for each leg. The hypotenuse scales by the same factor as the legs.
why.C: Correct — the new triangle is similar to the old one with scale factor 1.5, so every length, including the hypotenuse, grows by 50%.
why.D: This reports the scale factor, 1.5, as the increase. Multiplying by 1.5 is a 50% increase.

context: An isosceles triangle has two sides of length 10, and each of its base angles measures 30°. What is the area of the triangle?

why.A: This takes the two equal sides as a base and a height. They meet at 120°, not at a right angle.
why.B: This multiplies the base, 10√3, by the height, 5, and leaves out the 1/2.
why.C: This uses one equal side, 10, as the base with the height 5. The base of the triangle is the third side, 10√3.
why.D: Correct — the altitude to the base splits it into two 30°-60°-90° triangles with hypotenuse 10, so the height is 5 and each half of the base is 5√3. The area is (1/2)(10√3)(5).

context: The point (3, −7) is rotated 180° about the origin. What are the coordinates of its image?

why.A: Correct — a 180° rotation about the origin changes the sign of both coordinates.
why.B: This is a 90° counterclockwise rotation, (x, y) → (−y, x).
why.C: This is a reflection across the x-axis, which changes only the sign of y.
why.D: This is a reflection across the y-axis, which changes only the sign of x.

context: The point (−2, 5) is dilated by a scale factor of 3 with the center of dilation at the origin. What are the coordinates of its image?

why.A: This adds 3 to each coordinate, which is a translation, not a dilation.
why.B: Correct — a dilation centered at the origin multiplies both coordinates by the scale factor.
why.C: This multiplies only the x-coordinate by 3.
why.D: This divides by the scale factor, which shrinks the point toward the origin instead of stretching it away.

context: A rectangle has vertices at (−3, 2), (5, 2), (5, −4) and (−3, −4). What is its perimeter?

why.A: This is the area, 8 × 6, not the perimeter.
why.B: This adds one width and one height. A rectangle has two of each.
why.C: Correct — the width is 5 − (−3) = 8 and the height is 2 − (−4) = 6, so the perimeter is 2(8 + 6).
why.D: This finds the width as 5 − 3 = 2, dropping the sign of −3, and the height as 6: 2(2 + 6).

context: Reflecting across the line y = −x sends the point (3, −5) to which point?

why.A: This swaps the coordinates without changing their signs, the reflection across y = x.
why.B: This changes both signs without swapping, a 180° rotation about the origin.
why.C: This changes the sign of only one coordinate after swapping them.
why.D: Correct — reflecting across y = −x swaps the coordinates and changes both signs: (x, y) → (−y, −x).

context: The point (7, 3) is dilated by a scale factor of 2 with the center of dilation at (1, 1). What are the coordinates of its image?

why.A: Correct — the point is 6 right of and 2 above the center. Doubling gives 12 right and 4 above, landing at (1 + 12, 1 + 4).
why.B: This doubles the coordinates as if the center were the origin.
why.C: This doubles the distances from the center but forgets to add the center back.
why.D: This halves the distances from the center, a scale factor of 1/2.

context: A horizontal segment has its midpoint at (3, −1) and a length of 10. What are the coordinates of its endpoints?

why.A: This places each endpoint 10 from the midpoint, which makes the segment 20 long.
why.B: Correct — each endpoint is half the length, 5, to one side of the midpoint, along the horizontal line y = −1.
why.C: This runs the segment vertically. A horizontal segment keeps the same y-coordinate.
why.D: This centers the segment at x = 0 instead of at the midpoint’s x-coordinate, 3.

context: What is the area of the parallelogram with vertices (0, 0), (5, 0), (7, 4) and (2, 4)?

why.A: This takes half of base times height, the formula for a triangle.
why.B: This uses the width of the whole figure, from x = 0 to x = 7, as the base.
why.C: Correct — the base from (0, 0) to (5, 0) has length 5, and the opposite side lies on y = 4, so the height is 4.
why.D: This multiplies the two side lengths, 5 and √20. The slanted side is not the height.

context: Triangle ABC has vertices A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(k, −2), and it has a right angle at A. What is the value of k?

why.A: This gives AC a slope of 3/4, the reciprocal without the sign change, so AC is not perpendicular to AB.
why.B: This gives AC a slope of −4/3, changing the sign without taking the reciprocal.
why.C: This finds the run from A to C, 4, and forgets to add it to A’s x-coordinate, 1.
why.D: Correct — the slope of AB is 4/3, so AC needs slope −3/4. From A to C the rise is −3, so the run is 4 and k = 1 + 4.

context: What is the shortest distance from the origin to the line 3x + 4y = 20?

why.A: Correct — the line meets the axes at (20/3, 0) and (0, 5), and those intercepts form a right triangle with the origin whose hypotenuse is 25/3. The height to that hypotenuse is (20/3)(5) ÷ (25/3) = 4.
why.B: This is the distance to the y-intercept, (0, 5). The closest point on the line is where a perpendicular from the origin meets it.
why.C: This is the distance to the x-intercept, which is farther away than the y-intercept.
why.D: This reads the constant term as a distance. The coefficients 3 and 4 shrink it by a factor of √(3² + 4²) = 5.

context: Points A(0, 0), B(8, 0) and C(8, 6) form a right triangle. Point P lies on AC so that BP is perpendicular to AC. What are the coordinates of P?

why.A: This is the midpoint of AC. The foot of the perpendicular from B lands nearer to C.
why.B: Correct — AC lies along y = 0.75x and has length 10. AP = AB · cos A = 8(8/10) = 6.4, and moving 6.4 along AC from A means going 6.4(0.8) right and 6.4(0.6) up.
why.C: This uses the distance along AC, 6.4, as the x-coordinate instead of splitting it into its horizontal and vertical parts.
why.D: This swaps the coordinates. Every point on AC has a y-coordinate smaller than its x-coordinate.

context: A circle with center (3, 4) passes through the origin. Besides the origin, at what point does the circle cross the x-axis?

why.A: This is where the circle crosses the y-axis again, not the x-axis.
why.B: This is the point directly below the center, which lies inside the circle.
why.C: Correct — the radius is √(3² + 4²) = 5. On the x-axis, (x − 3)² + 4² = 25 gives x − 3 = ±3, so x = 0 or x = 6.
why.D: This adds the radius to the center’s x-coordinate. The center is not on the x-axis, so the crossing is closer.

context: A pyramid has a square base with sides of 6 meters and a height of 10 meters. What is its volume, in cubic meters?

why.A: This is base area times height, the volume of a prism with the same base. A pyramid holds one-third of that.
why.B: This uses the side, 6, in place of the base area, 6² = 36.
why.C: This takes one-half instead of one-third, the factor from the area of a triangle.
why.D: Correct — a pyramid holds one-third of base area times height: (1/3)(6²)(10) = 120.

context: A ball has a diameter of 12 inches. What is its volume, in cubic inches?

why.A: Correct — the radius is 6, and V = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π(216) = 288π.
why.B: This uses the diameter, 12, as the radius.
why.C: This multiplies by 4 but leaves out the division by 3 in 4/3.
why.D: This leaves out the 4/3 factor entirely, using πr³.

context: A metal block measures 2 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm and has a mass of 81 grams. What is its density, in grams per cubic centimeter? (Density is mass divided by volume.)

why.A: This divides by the sum of the dimensions, 2 + 3 + 5 = 10, instead of their product.
why.B: Correct — the volume is 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cubic centimeters, and 81 ÷ 30 = 2.7.
why.C: This divides the volume by the mass, turning the ratio upside down.
why.D: This multiplies the mass by the volume instead of dividing.

context: A circular pool with a radius of 10 feet is surrounded by a deck 2 feet wide all the way around. What is the area of the deck, in square feet?

why.A: This is the area of a circle whose radius is the deck’s width, 2. The deck is a ring, not a small circle.
why.B: This is the area inside the deck’s outer edge, which includes the pool.
why.C: Correct — the deck is the ring between a circle of radius 12 and the pool’s circle of radius 10: π(144) − π(100) = 44π.
why.D: This multiplies the pool’s circumference, 20π, by the deck’s width, 2. That undercounts the outer part of the ring, which is longer than the pool’s edge.

context: A grain silo is a cylinder with a radius of 3 meters and a height of 10 meters, topped by a hemisphere with the same radius. What is the total volume of the silo, in cubic meters?

why.A: This adds a whole sphere, 36π, instead of half of one.
why.B: This counts only the cylinder and leaves out the dome on top.
why.C: This gives the hemisphere a volume of 2πr³ = 54π, dropping the division by 3.
why.D: Correct — the cylinder holds π(3²)(10) = 90π and the hemisphere holds half of (4/3)π(3³), which is 18π.

context: A cylindrical tank with a radius of 2 meters stands upright and is being filled at a rate of 0.5π cubic meters per minute. How many meters does the water level rise each minute?

why.A: Correct — each meter of depth holds π(2²) = 4π cubic meters, so 0.5π cubic meters raises the level 0.5π ÷ 4π = 1/8 meter.
why.B: This divides by 2π, the base’s circumference per unit of radius, instead of its area, π(2²) = 4π.
why.C: This divides the base area by the fill rate, 4π ÷ 0.5π, which gives minutes per meter.
why.D: This keeps π in the rate but not in the base area, dividing 0.5π by 4. The two factors of π cancel.

context: How many cubes with 2-inch edges fit exactly inside a box that measures 6 inches by 8 inches by 10 inches?

why.A: This is the volume of the box in cubic inches, which counts 1-inch cubes.
why.B: Correct — 3 cubes fit along the 6-inch side, 4 along the 8-inch side and 5 along the 10-inch side: 3 × 4 × 5.
why.C: This divides the volume by 2, the edge of a cube, instead of by 8, the volume of a cube.
why.D: This divides the volume by 4, the area of one face of a cube, instead of by its volume.

context: Two similar cylinders have surface areas in the ratio 4 : 9. The larger cylinder has a volume of 270 cubic centimeters. What is the volume of the smaller cylinder, in cubic centimeters?

why.A: This applies the area ratio, 4/9, to the volume.
why.B: This applies the length ratio, 2/3, to the volume.
why.C: Correct — areas scale by the square of the length ratio, so the lengths are in the ratio 2 : 3. Volumes scale by its cube, 8 : 27, and 270 × 8/27 = 80.
why.D: This scales in the wrong direction, making the smaller cylinder’s volume larger.

context: A 4 × 4 × 4 cube is painted on all six faces and then cut into 64 unit cubes. How many of the unit cubes have paint on exactly two faces?

why.A: This counts the corner cubes, which have paint on three faces.
why.B: This counts all 4 cubes along each of the 12 edges, including the corners, which have three painted faces and are shared by edges.
why.C: This counts 3 cubes on each edge, removing only one of the two corners on each.
why.D: Correct — two-face cubes sit along the edges but not at the corners. Each of the 12 edges has 4 − 2 = 2 of them.

context: What is the length of the longest straight rod that fits inside a closed rectangular box measuring 3 feet by 4 feet by 12 feet?

why.A: Correct — the longest rod runs corner to opposite corner. The diagonal of the 3-by-4 floor is 5, and with the 12-foot height it makes √(5² + 12²) = 13.
why.B: This lays the rod along the longest edge. Tilting it across the box gives more room.
why.C: This is the diagonal of the 3-by-4 face only.
why.D: This adds the floor diagonal and the height, 5 + 12, instead of combining them with the Pythagorean theorem.

context: A rectangle measuring 4 inches by 6 inches is spun around its 6-inch side to sweep out a solid cylinder. What is the volume of the cylinder, in cubic inches?

why.A: This makes the 6-inch side the radius. Spinning around a side turns that side into the height.
why.B: Correct — the 6-inch side is the axis, so it becomes the height, and the 4-inch side sweeps around it as the radius: π(4²)(6).
why.C: This treats the 4-inch side as the diameter. It reaches from the axis to the edge, so it is the radius.
why.D: This takes one-third of πr²h, the formula for a cone. Spinning a rectangle sweeps out a cylinder.

context: A school orders 250 T-shirts, which are shipped in boxes of 24. Every box is full except possibly the last one. How many boxes are needed?

why.A: This rounds 10.4 down, which leaves 10 shirts without a box.
why.B: This is the exact quotient. A number of boxes must be a whole number.
why.C: Correct — 250 ÷ 24 ≈ 10.4, and ten full boxes hold only 240 shirts, so an eleventh box is needed for the other 10.
why.D: This multiplies 250 by 24 instead of dividing.

context: A shuttle bus leaves a hotel every 25 minutes, starting at 6:10 a.m. At what time does the 5th bus of the day leave?

why.A: This adds 5 intervals. The first bus leaves at 6:10 itself, so the 5th bus is only 4 intervals later.
why.B: This adds 3 intervals, which gives the 4th bus.
why.C: This adds 100 minutes as if it were 1 hour and 25 minutes.
why.D: Correct — the 5th bus leaves 4 intervals after the first: 4 × 25 = 100 minutes after 6:10 a.m.

context: A car travels 150 miles in 2 hours 30 minutes. What is its average speed, in miles per hour?

why.A: Correct — 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, and 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60.
why.B: This divides by 2 and ignores the extra 30 minutes.
why.C: This writes 2 hours 30 minutes as 2.3 hours. Thirty minutes is half an hour, 0.5.
why.D: This divides by 3, rounding the time up to 3 hours.

context: A baker’s fixed costs are $600 a month. Each cake costs $8 to make and sells for $20. How many cakes must the baker sell in a month to break even?

why.A: This divides the fixed costs by the selling price and ignores the $8 each cake costs to make.
why.B: Correct — each cake adds $20 − $8 = $12 toward the fixed costs, and 600 ÷ 12 = 50.
why.C: This divides the fixed costs by the cost of making a cake.
why.D: This divides by $28, adding the cost to the price instead of subtracting it.

context: Printer B prints 200 pages per hour and starts a job at 9:00 a.m. Printer A prints 300 pages per hour and starts its own copy of the job at 10:00 a.m. How many hours after 10:00 a.m. will the two printers have printed the same number of pages?

why.A: This is how long printer B has been running at that moment, counted from 9:00 a.m.
why.B: This is the head start. After 1 more hour, B still leads by 100 pages.
why.C: Correct — after t hours, A has printed 300t pages and B has printed 200(t + 1). Setting them equal gives 100t = 200, so t = 2.
why.D: This is the number of pages each printer has printed when they are even.

context: A hose fills a pool at 12 gallons per minute. The pool holds 9,000 gallons. How many hours does it take to fill the empty pool?

why.A: This is the time in minutes. It still needs converting to hours.
why.B: This converts the rate the wrong way, dividing 12 by 60 to get 0.2 gallon per minute.
why.C: This misplaces the decimal point when dividing 750 by 60.
why.D: Correct — 9,000 ÷ 12 = 750 minutes, and 750 ÷ 60 = 12.5 hours.

context: Dana’s hourly pay rose from $15 to $18. How many hours must she work now to earn what she used to earn in 30 hours?

why.A: Correct — she used to earn 30 × $15 = $450, and $450 ÷ $18 = 25 hours.
why.B: This scales the hours up by 18/15. A higher rate means fewer hours for the same pay.
why.C: This subtracts the $3 raise from the hours.
why.D: This adds the $3 raise to the hours.

context: A shop buys 60 shirts at $8 each. It sells three-fourths of them at $15 each and the rest at $6 each. What is the shop’s total profit?

why.A: This is the total sales revenue before the cost of the shirts is subtracted.
why.B: Correct — sales bring in 45 × $15 + 15 × $6 = $675 + $90 = $765, and the shirts cost 60 × $8 = $480.
why.C: This sells all 60 shirts at $15. Only 45 of them sold at that price.
why.D: This counts the profit on the 45 shirts sold at $15 and ignores the $2 lost on each of the other 15.

context: A driver covers the first 60 miles of a 120-mile trip at 30 miles per hour. How fast must she drive the remaining 60 miles to average 40 miles per hour for the whole trip?

why.A: This makes the two speeds average to 40. The slower half takes more time, so it counts for more of the average.
why.B: This drives the second half at the target average, which cannot make up for the slow first half.
why.C: Correct — averaging 40 mph over 120 miles takes 3 hours. The first half took 60 ÷ 30 = 2 hours, leaving 1 hour for the last 60 miles.
why.D: This adds 15 mph, half the gap between 30 and 60, without working out the time left.

context: A train 200 meters long travels at 20 meters per second. How many seconds pass from the moment its front enters a 400-meter bridge until its rear leaves the bridge?

why.A: This counts only the bridge length. When the front reaches the far end, the rest of the train is still on the bridge.
why.B: This counts only the train’s length.
why.C: This stops when the middle of the train leaves the bridge, 400 + 100 meters from the start.
why.D: Correct — the front must travel the bridge’s 400 meters plus the train’s own 200 meters before the rear clears it: 600 ÷ 20.

context: The pages of a book are numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on. Printing all the page numbers uses 192 digits in total. How many pages does the book have?

why.A: Correct — pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits and pages 10 to 99 use 180 more, 189 in all. The last 3 digits are one 3-digit page, page 100.
why.B: This divides 192 by 2, as if every page number had two digits.
why.C: This divides 192 by 3, as if every page number had three digits.
why.D: This stops at the last two-digit page, which uses only 189 digits.

context: The function T(m) = 1.5m + 20 gives the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, of a liquid m minutes after a heater is switched on. What does the statement T(4) = 26 mean?

why.A: This swaps the input and the output. The number inside the parentheses is the time.
why.B: Correct — the input m = 4 is the time in minutes, and the output 26 is the temperature at that time.
why.C: T(4) is a single reading, not a rate. The rate is the 1.5 degrees per minute.
why.D: The rise per minute is 1.5, the coefficient of m, not the input 4.

context: If f(x) = x² − 1 and g(x) = 2x + 3, what is the value of f(2) · g(2)?

why.A: This adds f(2) and g(2) instead of multiplying them.
why.B: This is f(g(2)) = f(7) = 48, a composition rather than a product.
why.C: Correct — f(2) = 3 and g(2) = 7, and their product is 21.
why.D: This is g(f(2)) = g(3) = 9, a composition in the other order.

context: Which of the following functions satisfies f(−x) = f(x) for every value of x?

why.A: Here f(−x) = −x³, the opposite of f(x), not the same.
why.B: This parabola is shifted 2 units left, so it is symmetric about x = −2 rather than the y-axis. For example, f(1) = 9 but f(−1) = 1.
why.C: Here f(−x) = −2x, which equals f(x) only when x = 0.
why.D: Correct — (−x)² = x², so replacing x with −x leaves x² + 4 unchanged.

context: A function f takes the values f(0) = 5, f(1) = 15, f(2) = 45 and f(3) = 135. Which of the following could define f?

why.A: Correct — each output is 3 times the one before, so f is exponential with growth factor 3, and f(0) = 5 is the starting value.
why.B: This swaps the starting value and the growth factor. It gives f(0) = 3.
why.C: This uses the first jump, from 5 to 15, as a constant rate. The next jump is 30, so the change is not constant.
why.D: This starts one factor of 3 too high, giving f(0) = 15.

context: On which interval is the function f(x) = −(x − 1)² + 4 increasing?

why.A: This is where an upward-opening parabola rises. The leading negative sign flips it, so it falls there.
why.B: Correct — the parabola opens downward with its vertex at x = 1, so it rises until x = 1 and falls after.
why.C: This uses the maximum value, 4, as an x-value. The turning point is at x = 1.
why.D: This mixes up the vertex’s y-coordinate with its x-coordinate and also reverses the direction.

context: A theater has 120 seats. The function R(n) = 15n gives the ticket revenue, in dollars, when n tickets are sold for one show. Which set is the most reasonable domain of R?
