choices.text: all whole numbers, with no upper limit

why.A: This allows fractions of a ticket, such as n = 2.5, which cannot be sold.
why.B: This is the set of possible revenues, 15 × 120 = 1,800 at most, which describes outputs, not inputs.
why.C: Correct — n counts tickets, so it is a whole number, and it can run from none sold up to the 120 seats.
why.D: This ignores the 120-seat limit on how many tickets can be sold.

context: If f(x) = 2x − 3, what is the value of f(f⁻¹(9) + 1)?

why.A: This cancels f against f⁻¹ and adds the 1 afterward. The 1 is added inside, before f is applied.
why.B: This uses f(9) = 15 in place of f⁻¹(9), then finds f(16).
why.C: This cancels f against f⁻¹ and drops the + 1 altogether.
why.D: Correct — f⁻¹(9) is the input with 2x − 3 = 9, which is 6. Then f(6 + 1) = f(7) = 11.

context: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x + k for x < 3 and f(x) = x² − 1 for x ≥ 3. For what value of k does the graph of f have no break at x = 3?

why.A: Correct — at x = 3 the right piece gives 3² − 1 = 8, so the left piece must approach 8 as well: 2(3) + k = 8, so k = 2.
why.B: This is the height where the pieces must meet, not the value of k.
why.C: This leaves out the − 1, taking the right piece’s value at x = 3 as 9.
why.D: This adds 6 to 8 instead of subtracting it.

context: For f(x) = x² − 4x + 1, how many real values of x satisfy f(x) = −3?

why.A: This assumes a horizontal line always crosses a parabola twice. Here −3 is the parabola’s minimum value, so it is touched once.
why.B: Correct — x² − 4x + 1 = −3 becomes x² − 4x + 4 = 0, or (x − 2)² = 0. The line y = −3 touches the parabola only at its vertex, (2, −3).
why.C: This treats −3 as below the parabola. The lowest value of f is exactly −3, so it is reached.
why.D: An equation with a squared term has at most two real solutions.

context: The graph of y = f(x) crosses the x-axis only at x = −1 and x = 5. The function g is defined by g(x) = f(x + 2) − 3. What are all the solutions of g(x) = −3?

why.A: This shifts the zeros 2 units right. Adding 2 inside f shifts the graph left.
why.B: This ignores the shift inside f and uses the zeros of f itself.
why.C: Correct — g(x) = −3 means f(x + 2) = 0, so x + 2 = −1 or x + 2 = 5.
why.D: This shifts the zeros by 3, the vertical change, instead of by 2.

context: If f(x) = 3x − 5 and g(x) = f(2x + 1), what is the slope of the graph of y = g(x)?

why.A: This is the slope of f. Feeding in 2x + 1 makes the input change twice as fast.
why.B: This is the slope of the inner expression 2x + 1 alone.
why.C: This adds the two slopes, 3 + 2, instead of multiplying them.
why.D: Correct — g(x) = 3(2x + 1) − 5 = 6x − 2, so each unit step in x moves the output 3 × 2 = 6 units.

context: A round pizza is cut into 8 equal slices by straight cuts through its center. What is the measure of the angle at the tip of each slice?

why.A: Correct — the tips of the 8 slices fill the full 360° around the center, so each is 360° ÷ 8.
why.B: This counts the 4 straight cuts as 4 slices. Each cut through the center makes two slice edges.
why.C: This divides 360° by 16, twice the number of slices.
why.D: This is the interior angle of a regular octagon, a different angle from the one at the center.

context: Through how many degrees does the hour hand of a clock turn from 1:00 to 3:30?

why.A: This uses the minute hand’s rate, 6° a minute, for all 150 minutes.
why.B: Correct — the hour hand turns 360° in 12 hours, or 30° an hour, and 2.5 × 30° = 75°.
why.C: This counts only the 2 whole hours and drops the half hour.
why.D: This measures from 12:00 to 3:30, 3.5 hours, instead of starting at 1:00.

context: Angle ABC measures 128°. Ray BD lies inside the angle and splits it so that angle ABD and angle DBC are in the ratio 3 : 1. What is the measure of angle DBC?

why.A: This is angle ABD, the 3-part piece.
why.B: This divides 128° by 3, forgetting the 1 part in the ratio.
why.C: Correct — the angle is split into 3 + 1 = 4 equal parts of 32°, and angle DBC is 1 part.
why.D: This splits a straight angle, 180°, into 4 parts. The angle being split is 128°.

context: Three straight lines pass through one point and form six angles around it. Two angles next to each other measure 48° and 71°. What is the measure of the angle next to the 71° angle on its other side?

why.A: This treats the 71° angle and the unknown as a linear pair. With three lines, a straight line is split into three angles, not two.
why.B: This assumes the unknown is vertical to the 48° angle. The angle vertical to 48° is three positions away, not next to the 71° angle.
why.C: This subtracts from 360° as if only three angles filled the whole turn.
why.D: Correct — any three angles in a row around the point lie along a straight line, so 48° + 71° + x = 180°.

context: Lines ℓ and m are parallel. Point P is on ℓ, and points Q and R are on m. Side PQ makes a 50° angle with ℓ, and angle QPR of triangle PQR measures 70°, so the angles at P along line ℓ are 50°, 70° and a third angle between PR and ℓ. What is the measure of angle PRQ?

why.A: Correct — the three angles at P along ℓ form a straight angle, so the angle between PR and ℓ is 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°. Angle PRQ is alternate interior to it across the parallel lines, so it is also 60°.
why.B: This is angle PQR, the alternate interior partner of the 50° angle at P, not the angle at R.
why.C: This repeats angle QPR, the triangle’s angle at P.
why.D: This is the supplement of the correct angle, the angle between PR and line m on the other side of R.

context: A ship sails on a compass bearing of 070° and then turns onto a bearing of 160°. (Bearings are measured clockwise from north.) Through what angle, and in which direction, did the ship turn?

why.A: The size is right, but a larger bearing is reached by turning clockwise.
why.B: Correct — bearings increase clockwise, and 160° − 70° = 90°.
why.C: This adds the two bearings instead of subtracting.
why.D: This finds 180° − 70°, treating the new bearing as due south.

context: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon. What is the measure of angle FAC?

why.A: This is the whole interior angle FAB, which includes angle BAC as well.
why.B: This is angle FAC’s neighbor in the equilateral triangle ACE, angle CAE.
why.C: Correct — each interior angle is 120°. Triangle ABC is isosceles with a 120° angle at B, so angle BAC = 30°, leaving 120° − 30° = 90° for angle FAC.
why.D: This is angle BAC, the other part of the interior angle at A.

context: The five exterior angles of a pentagon, one at each vertex, measure x°, 2x°, 3x°, 4x° and 5x°. What is the measure of the pentagon’s largest interior angle?

why.A: This is the largest exterior angle, 5x. The largest interior angle pairs with the smallest exterior angle.
why.B: This uses 540°, the interior total, as the exterior total, so x = 36.
why.C: This is each interior angle of a regular pentagon. This pentagon’s angles are all different.
why.D: Correct — exterior angles total 360°, so 15x = 360 and x = 24. The largest interior angle sits beside the smallest exterior angle: 180° − 24° = 156°.

context: A ray of light strikes a flat mirror, making a 35° angle with the mirror’s surface, and reflects so that it leaves at the same angle to the surface on the other side. What is the angle between the incoming ray and the reflected ray?

why.A: Correct — the two 35° angles and the angle between the rays sit along the straight mirror, so the angle between the rays is 180° − 70°.
why.B: This adds the two 35° angles. Those are the angles with the mirror; the angle between the rays is what remains of the straight angle.
why.C: This subtracts only one 35° angle from 180°.
why.D: This takes the angle with the mirror as the angle between the rays.

context: Two regular octagons and one other regular polygon meet at a single point, fitting together with no gaps or overlaps. How many sides does the other polygon have?

why.A: A third octagon would need 135°, which is more than the 90° left.
why.B: Correct — each octagon’s interior angle is 135°, so the two use 270°. The last 90° must be one interior angle of the third polygon, which is a square.
why.C: This makes the gap 120°, a hexagon’s angle, as if each octagon took 120°.
why.D: This leaves 60° for the third polygon, as if each octagon’s angle were 150°.

context: For how many whole numbers n from 3 through 12 is each interior angle of a regular n-sided polygon a whole number of degrees?

why.A: This counts every n from 3 through 12. For 7 and 11 the angle is a repeating decimal.
why.B: This checks which n divide 180 instead of 360, which leaves out n = 8, whose angle is exactly 135°.
why.C: Correct — each interior angle is 180° − 360°/n, which is whole exactly when n divides 360. From 3 through 12 that holds for 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12, but not 7 or 11.
why.D: This counts only the polygons that tile a flat surface by themselves, n = 3, 4 and 6.

context: How many terms are in the arithmetic sequence 12, 15, 18, …, 99?

why.A: This counts the steps between terms. There is always one more term than there are steps.
why.B: This divides the last term by 3, counting the multiples of 3 from 3 up, not from 12.
why.C: This subtracts the first term from the last without dividing by the common difference.
why.D: Correct — the terms climb from 12 to 99 in steps of 3, which is (99 − 12) ÷ 3 = 29 steps, and 29 steps join 30 terms.

context: The number of seats in row n of a theater is aₙ = 2n + 14. How many seats are in row 1, and how many more seats does each row have than the row in front of it?

why.A: Correct — row 1 has 2(1) + 14 = 16 seats, and each step up in n adds 2 seats.
why.B: This reads the constant 14 as the first term. It is the value at n = 0, a row that does not exist.
why.C: This swaps the roles of the coefficient and the constant.
why.D: This finds row 1 correctly but takes the constant 14 as the step between rows.

context: The nth term of a geometric sequence is aₙ = 3 · 2ⁿ⁻¹. What is the 6th term?

why.A: This uses 2⁶ and ignores the − 1 in the exponent, landing on the 7th term.
why.B: Correct — the exponent is 6 − 1 = 5, and 3 · 2⁵ = 3 · 32 = 96.
why.C: This multiplies 2 by 5 instead of raising 2 to the 5th power.
why.D: This multiplies 3 by 2 first and raises 6 to the 5th power. The exponent applies only to the 2.

context: What is the value of ∑ (3k − 1) for k = 1 to 10?

why.A: This is only the last term, the value at k = 10, not the sum of all ten terms.
why.B: This adds 3k from 1 to 10 but drops the − 1 that is taken away in every term.
why.C: Correct — the terms are 2, 5, 8, …, 29, and ten of them average (2 + 29) ÷ 2 = 15.5, so the sum is 155.
why.D: This subtracts the 1 only once instead of once for each of the ten terms.

context: In a geometric sequence, the 1st term is 2 and the 3rd term is 18. What are all the possible values of the 2nd term?

why.A: This keeps only the positive square root. A ratio of −3 gives 2, −6, 18, which also works.
why.B: This takes the number halfway between 2 and 18, the middle term of an arithmetic sequence.
why.C: This sets the 2nd term squared equal to 18 alone. In a geometric sequence the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbors, 2 × 18 = 36.
why.D: Correct — the ratio r satisfies 2r² = 18, so r² = 9 and r = 3 or r = −3. The 2nd term 2r is then 6 or −6.

context: Nadia saves $5 in week 1, $8 in week 2, $11 in week 3, and so on, adding $3 more each week. How many dollars has she saved in all after 10 weeks?

why.A: Correct — the week-10 amount is 5 + 9(3) = 32, and the ten amounts average (5 + 32) ÷ 2 = 18.5, so she saves 10 × 18.5 = 185.
why.B: This is only what she saves in week 10, not the total.
why.C: This multiplies 10 by the sum of the first and last amounts without halving it.
why.D: This adds $3 only once per week to a flat $5, as if the extra did not build up from week to week.

context: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 7 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4 for n ≥ 2. Which formula gives the nth term directly?

why.A: This uses 7 as the constant, but at n = 1 that gives 11. The 7 must be the value at n = 1.
why.B: Correct — the terms are 7, 11, 15, …, so aₙ = 7 + 4(n − 1) = 4n + 3.
why.C: This swaps the first term and the common difference.
why.D: This treats the sequence as geometric. Adding 4 each time is arithmetic.

context: What is the sum of all the two-digit positive multiples of 7?

why.A: This counts 12 terms, (98 − 14) ÷ 7, forgetting to add 1 for the first term.
why.B: This multiplies 13 by 14 + 98 without halving it to find the average.
why.C: Correct — the multiples run 14, 21, …, 98, which is 13 terms, and their average is (14 + 98) ÷ 2 = 56, so the sum is 13 × 56.
why.D: This includes 7, which has only one digit.

context: A ball is dropped from a height of 12 meters. After each bounce it rises to 3/4 of the height it just fell from, and it keeps bouncing forever in theory. What is the total vertical distance, in meters, the ball travels?

why.A: This finds 12 ÷ (1 − 3/4), counting each bounce height only once, as if the ball never came back down.
why.B: This doubles 48, counting the first 12-meter drop twice, though the ball never rose to it.
why.C: This adds only the rises after the first drop.
why.D: Correct — it falls 12, then rises and falls 9, 6.75, … twice each. The rises sum to 9 ÷ (1 − 3/4) = 36, so the total is 12 + 2(36) = 84.

context: An infinite geometric series has a sum of 27, and its 2nd term is 6. What are all the possible values of its 1st term?

why.A: Correct — a/(1 − r) = 27 and ar = 6 give 27r(1 − r) = 6, so 9r² − 9r + 2 = 0 and r = 1/3 or 2/3. The 1st term 27(1 − r) is then 18 or 9.
why.B: This finds r = 1/3 but misses the second root, r = 2/3, which also gives a sum of 27.
why.C: This finds r = 2/3 but misses the second root, r = 1/3.
why.D: This subtracts the 2nd term from the sum, as if the series had only two terms.

context: In an arithmetic sequence, the 5th term plus the 15th term equals 50. What is the sum of the first 19 terms?

why.A: This multiplies 19 by 50, the sum of a pair, instead of by 25, the average term.
why.B: Correct — the 5th and 15th terms sit equally far from the 10th term, so the 10th term is 50 ÷ 2 = 25. The 19 terms are centered on the 10th, so their sum is 19 × 25.
why.C: This uses 20 terms, as if the 10th term were the middle of 20.
why.D: This multiplies the average term by 10, counting only half the terms.

context: A circle has center (1, 2) and radius 5. Which of the following points lies outside the circle?

why.A: Its distance from the center is √(3² + 3²) = √18 ≈ 4.24, less than 5, so it is inside.
why.B: Its distance from the center is √(4² + 3²) = 5 exactly, so it lies on the circle, not outside it.
why.C: Correct — its distance from the center is √(4² + 4²) = √32 ≈ 5.66, which is more than the radius 5.
why.D: It is 5 units to the right of the center, exactly the radius, so it lies on the circle.

context: Minor arc AB of a circle measures 72°. What fraction of the circle’s circumference is arc AB?

why.A: This divides by 180° instead of the full 360°.
why.B: This reads 72° as 72 percent, which is 72/100.
why.C: This is the fraction for the major arc, the 288° left over.
why.D: Correct — a full circle is 360°, and 72/360 = 1/5.

context: A diameter of a circle has endpoints (−1, 3) and (5, −5). Which equation represents the circle?

why.A: Correct — the center is the midpoint, (2, −1). The diameter is √(6² + 8²) = 10, so the radius is 5 and r² = 25.
why.B: This uses the square of the diameter, 10, instead of the radius.
why.C: This flips the signs of the center. In (x − h)², the center’s x-coordinate is h.
why.D: This puts the radius itself on the right side instead of its square.

context: In a circle graph of a family’s monthly budget of $2,400, the rent sector has a central angle of 126°. How many dollars a month go to rent?

why.A: This treats 126° as 126 percent, multiplying 2,400 by 1.26.
why.B: Correct — the rent sector is 126/360 = 35% of the circle, and 35% of $2,400 is $840.
why.C: This divides by 180° instead of the 360° in a full circle.
why.D: This is the rest of the budget, the 234° outside the rent sector.

context: Line PT is tangent to a circle with center O at point T. If angle TOP measures 58°, what is the measure of angle OPT?

why.A: This treats triangle OTP as isosceles, matching the angle at P to the angle at O.
why.B: This is the supplement of 58°, as if angles TOP and OPT formed a straight line.
why.C: Correct — a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so angle OTP = 90° and angle OPT = 180° − 90° − 58°.
why.D: This is angle OTP, the right angle at the point of tangency, not the angle at P.

context: The area of a circle, in square units, is numerically equal to its circumference, in units. What is the radius of the circle?

why.A: This is the diameter of the circle, not its radius.
why.B: This sets πr² equal to πr, leaving out the 2 in the circumference formula 2πr.
why.C: This sets 2πr² equal to πr, putting the 2 on the wrong side.
why.D: Correct — πr² = 2πr, and dividing both sides by πr gives r = 2.

context: Point P is the point on the circle (x − 3)² + (y − 4)² = 4 that is closest to the origin. How far is P from the origin?

why.A: Correct — the center (3, 4) is 5 units from the origin, and the nearest point of the circle is one radius, 2, closer.
why.B: This is the distance to the center, not to the nearest point on the circle.
why.C: This adds the radius, giving the farthest point of the circle from the origin.
why.D: This subtracts 4, reading the r² on the right side of the equation as the radius.

context: Points C and D lie on a circle with center O, on the same side of chord AB. Angle ACB measures (3x + 10)°, and angle ADB measures (5x − 14)°. What is the measure of central angle AOB?

why.A: This is each inscribed angle. A central angle is twice an inscribed angle on the same arc.
why.B: Correct — inscribed angles on the same arc are equal, so 3x + 10 = 5x − 14 and x = 12. Each inscribed angle is 46°, and the central angle on the same arc is twice that.
why.C: This halves the inscribed angle instead of doubling it.
why.D: This is the value of x, not an angle in the figure.

context: In a circle with radius 6, chord AB subtends a central angle of 90°. What is the area of the smaller region between chord AB and arc AB?

why.A: This is the whole sector, including the triangle between the chord and the center.
why.B: This subtracts 6 × 6 for the triangle, forgetting the 1/2.
why.C: Correct — the 90° sector has area (1/4)π(6²) = 9π, and the right triangle inside it has area (1/2)(6)(6) = 18. The region is the difference.
why.D: This subtracts the triangle from the whole circle instead of from the sector.

context: At how many points does the line y = 2x + 10 meet the circle x² + y² = 20?

why.A: This assumes a line through a circle’s region always cuts it twice. The equation has a double root.
why.B: This compares the y-intercept 10 with the radius and concludes the line misses. The line’s slope brings it to the circle.
why.C: A line and a circle can meet at most twice, since substituting gives a quadratic.
why.D: Correct — substituting gives x² + (2x + 10)² = 20, or 5x² + 40x + 80 = 0, which is 5(x + 4)² = 0. The single root means the line is tangent at (−4, 2).

context: Two circles share the same center. A chord of the larger circle is 16 units long and touches the smaller circle at exactly one point. What is the area of the ring between the two circles?

why.A: Correct — the radius to the point of contact bisects the chord at a right angle, so R² − r² = 8² = 64, and the ring’s area is π(R² − r²).
why.B: This squares the whole chord, 16, instead of half of it.
why.C: This finds R² − r² but leaves out the factor π in the area.
why.D: This multiplies π by the half-chord 8 without squaring it.

context: A theater sold 120 tickets for a total of $780. Adult tickets cost $8 and child tickets cost $5. If a is the number of adult tickets and c is the number of child tickets, which system models the sales?

why.A: This swaps the two totals. The 120 counts tickets and the 780 counts dollars.
why.B: Correct — one equation counts tickets and the other counts dollars, with each price attached to its own kind of ticket.
why.C: This attaches each price to the wrong kind of ticket.
why.D: This adds the two prices and charges $13 for every ticket, which ignores that the kinds cost different amounts.

context: To solve the system 2x + 3y = 7 and 5x − 3y = 14 by elimination, which single step removes y?

choices.text: Subtract the second equation from the first.
Multiply the first equation by 5, then add.
Add the two equations as they stand.
Multiply by 5 and by 2 to match x, then subtract.

why.A: Subtracting gives 3y − (−3y) = 6y, which doubles the y-terms instead of removing them.
why.B: This gives 15y − 3y = 12y, so y remains. Nothing cancels.
why.C: Correct — the y-terms are 3y and −3y, which cancel when the equations are added, leaving 7x = 21.
why.D: Multiplying the first by 5 and the second by 2 makes both x-terms 10x, so it removes x, not y.

context: The monthly costs of two phone plans are graphed with minutes of calls on the x-axis and cost, in dollars, on the y-axis. The two graphs intersect at (40, 30). What does this point tell you?

choices.text: Both plans cost $40 for 30 minutes of calls.
One plan costs $40 and the other costs $30.
The two plans differ in cost by $10.
Both plans cost $30 for 40 minutes of calls.

why.A: This swaps the coordinates. The x-value is minutes and the y-value is dollars.
why.B: This reads the two coordinates as the two plans’ costs. The point is shared by both graphs.
why.C: This subtracts the coordinates. At the intersection the plans cost exactly the same.
why.D: Correct — the intersection is the one input where both plans give the same output: at x = 40 minutes, both costs are y = 30 dollars.

context: A jar holds only nickels and dimes: 30 coins worth $2.10 in all. How many of the coins are dimes?

why.A: Correct — with d dimes there are 30 − d nickels, so 5(30 − d) + 10d = 210 cents. That gives 150 + 5d = 210, so d = 12.
why.B: This is the number of nickels, 30 − 12.
why.C: This divides $2.10 by 10 cents, as if every coin were a dime.
why.D: This splits the 30 coins evenly, but 15 dimes and 15 nickels are worth $2.25, not $2.10.

context: A rectangle has a perimeter of 46 centimeters, and its length is 5 centimeters less than 3 times its width. What is the length of the rectangle, in centimeters?

why.A: This is the width. The question asks for the length.
why.B: Correct — l + w = 23 and l = 3w − 5, so 4w − 5 = 23, w = 7 and l = 3(7) − 5 = 16.
why.C: This is half the perimeter, the length and width added together.
why.D: This finds the width, 7, and triples it but forgets to subtract the 5.

context: The point (2, 3) is a solution of both ax + y = 11 and 2x − by = 7. What is the value of a + b?

why.A: This drops the sign when solving 4 − 3b = 7, taking b = 1.
why.B: This is a alone. The question asks for a + b.
why.C: Correct — 2a + 3 = 11 gives a = 4, and 4 − 3b = 7 gives b = −1, so a + b = 3.
why.D: This substitutes x = 3 and y = 2, reversing the coordinates of the point.

context: Line p passes through (0, 4) and (2, 10). Line q is y = 3x − 5. How many solutions does the system made of the equations of lines p and q have?

why.A: This assumes two different lines always cross. Lines with equal slopes and different intercepts never do.
why.B: This follows from equal slopes only if the intercepts also match. Here they are 4 and −5.
why.C: Two straight lines can share at most one point unless they are the same line. Two crossings happen with a line and a curve.
why.D: Correct — line p has slope (10 − 4) ÷ 2 = 3, the same as line q, but its y-intercept is 4, not −5. Parallel lines never meet.

context: In the xy-plane, a region is made of all points that satisfy x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + 2y ≤ 8 and y ≤ 3. What is the area of the region?

why.A: Correct — the corners are (0, 0), (8, 0), (2, 3) and (0, 3), a trapezoid with parallel sides 8 and 2 and height 3, so the area is (8 + 2) ÷ 2 × 3.
why.B: This ignores y ≤ 3 and finds the triangle under x + 2y = 8, with legs 8 and 4.
why.C: This finds the rectangle 8 wide and 3 tall, ignoring the slanted edge.
why.D: This adds the parallel sides and multiplies by the height without halving.

context: Pens cost $3 each and notebooks cost $5 each. Leo spends exactly $41 and buys at least one of each. How many different combinations of pens and notebooks could he have bought?

why.A: This stops at the first combination found, 12 pens and 1 notebook.
why.B: Correct — 41 − 5n must be a positive multiple of 3. That happens for n = 1, 4 and 7 notebooks, with 12, 7 and 2 pens.
why.C: This counts every number of notebooks from 1 to 8 that costs no more than $41, without checking that the rest buys whole pens.
why.D: This counts every number of pens from 1 to 13 that costs no more than $41, without checking the notebooks.

context: Which of the following lists every solution (x, y) of the system y = |x| and y = 2x − 3?

why.A: This keeps x = 1 from the x < 0 case without checking it. At x = 1, 2x − 3 = −1, not 1.
why.B: This keeps the rejected case and drops the valid one.
why.C: Correct — for x ≥ 0, x = 2x − 3 gives x = 3. For x < 0, −x = 2x − 3 gives x = 1, which is not negative, so it is rejected.
why.D: This treats the V-shaped graph as if a line with slope 2 could not reach it. The line crosses the right branch once.

context: The system y = 2x + 1 and y = x² + c has no real solution. Which describes all possible values of c?

why.A: This reverses the inequality. For c < 2 the discriminant is positive and the graphs cross twice.
why.B: This moves c across but forgets the 1 from the line, solving 4 − 4c < 0.
why.C: This is the case where the line just touches the parabola, which is one solution, not none.
why.D: Correct — x² + c = 2x + 1 gives x² − 2x + (c − 1) = 0, with discriminant 4 − 4(c − 1) = 8 − 4c. There is no real solution when 8 − 4c < 0, so c > 2.

context: Which of the following quadratic functions has a graph that opens downward and crosses the y-axis at 3?

why.A: Correct — the negative leading coefficient makes it open downward, and at x = 0 the value is 3.
why.B: This crosses the y-axis at 3, but its positive leading coefficient makes it open upward.
why.C: This opens downward, but its y-intercept is the constant 1. The 3 is the coefficient of x.
why.D: This opens upward and passes through the origin. The leading 3 is not the y-intercept.

context: What are all the solutions of 2x² = 50?

why.A: This keeps only the positive square root. (−5)² is also 25.
why.B: Correct — dividing by 2 gives x² = 25, and both 5 and −5 square to 25.
why.C: This divides by 2 but forgets to take the square root.
why.D: This takes the square root of 50 without dividing by 2 first.

context: The height, in feet, of a ball t seconds after it is thrown is h(t) = −16t² + 48t + 4. What does the 4 represent?

choices.text: The ball’s greatest height is 4 feet.
The ball is in the air for 4 seconds.
The ball’s height at the moment it is thrown is 4 feet.
The ball is thrown upward at 4 feet per second.

why.A: The greatest height is at the vertex, t = 1.5, where h = 40 feet.
why.B: The time in the air comes from solving h(t) = 0, not from the constant term.
why.C: Correct — at t = 0 the first two terms are 0, so h(0) = 4.
why.D: The starting upward speed is the coefficient of t, 48 feet per second.

context: Which of the following is a factored form of 3x² + 10x − 8?

why.A: This has the signs reversed. It expands to 3x² − 10x − 8.
why.B: This pairs the factors of 8 the other way. It expands to 3x² + 2x − 8.
why.C: This pairs the factors the other way and reverses the signs. It expands to 3x² − 2x − 8.
why.D: Correct — the outer and inner products are 12x and −2x, which add to 10x, and the last terms multiply to −8.

context: What are the solutions of x² − 4x − 1 = 0?

why.A: Correct — the quadratic formula gives (4 ± √(16 + 4)) ÷ 2 = (4 ± 2√5) ÷ 2 = 2 ± √5.
why.B: This uses b = −4 directly instead of −b = 4 at the front of the formula.
why.C: This finds 4 ± √20 but leaves out the division by 2a = 2.
why.D: This takes c as +1, so the discriminant becomes 16 − 4 = 12.

context: What are all the solutions of x + 6/x = 5?

why.A: This factors correctly but flips the signs when setting each factor to 0.
why.B: Correct — multiplying by x gives x² + 6 = 5x, so x² − 5x + 6 = 0 and (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0.
why.C: This uses factors of 6 without checking that they add to 5.
why.D: This moves the 6 to the wrong side, solving x² − 5x − 6 = 0.

context: A square garden is surrounded by a path 2 meters wide. The garden and path together cover 196 square meters. What is the side length, in meters, of the garden alone?

why.A: This subtracts the path width only once. The path runs along both sides of the garden.
why.B: This is the side of the outer square, garden and path together.
why.C: Correct — the outer square has side √196 = 14, and the path takes 2 meters off each of the two sides, so the garden’s side is 14 − 4.
why.D: This divides 196 by 4 as if the area were a perimeter.

context: What is the sum of all the positive solutions of x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0?

why.A: This adds the values of x², 1 + 4, without taking square roots.
why.B: This adds all four solutions, including the negative ones.
why.C: This counts the solutions instead of adding the positive ones.
why.D: Correct — with u = x², the equation is u² − 5u + 4 = 0, so u = 1 or u = 4. Then x = ±1 or x = ±2, and the positive solutions add to 1 + 2.

context: If x + 1/x = 5, what is the value of x² + 1/x²?

why.A: Correct — squaring gives x² + 2(x)(1/x) + 1/x² = 25, and the middle term is 2, so x² + 1/x² = 23.
why.B: This squares each term separately and forgets the middle term, 2.
why.C: This adds the middle term 2 instead of subtracting it.
why.D: This doubles 5 instead of squaring the expression.

context: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c passes through (0, 5), (1, 4) and (−1, 10). What is the x-coordinate of its vertex?

why.A: This drops the negative sign in −b/(2a).
why.B: Correct — c = 5, then a + b = −1 and a − b = 5, so a = 2 and b = −3. The vertex is at x = −b/(2a) = 3/4.
why.C: This divides by a instead of 2a.
why.D: This is the value of a, not the vertex.

context: Which describes all values of x for which (x − 1)(x + 3) ≥ 5?

why.A: This is where the product is at most 5. An upward parabola is at or above 0 outside its roots.
why.B: This uses the roots of (x − 1)(x + 3) = 0, ignoring the 5.
why.C: Correct — the inequality becomes x² + 2x − 8 ≥ 0, or (x + 4)(x − 2) ≥ 0, which holds outside the roots.
why.D: This keeps only the right branch and misses values such as x = −5.

context: If cos θ = 0.4 and θ is acute, what is the value of sec θ?

why.A: This subtracts cos θ from 1, as if the secant were a complement. It is a reciprocal.
why.B: This is cos θ itself, not its reciprocal.
why.C: This is 1/sin θ, the cosecant, with sin θ = √(1 − 0.16) ≈ 0.92.
why.D: Correct — sec θ = 1/cos θ = 1/0.4 = 2.5.

context: A right triangle has legs of length 8 and 15. Angle θ is opposite the leg of length 8. What is cot θ?

why.A: Correct — cot θ = adjacent/opposite = 15/8, the reciprocal of tan θ.
why.B: This is tan θ, opposite over adjacent. The cotangent is its reciprocal.
why.C: This is csc θ, hypotenuse over opposite. The hypotenuse is √(8² + 15²) = 17.
why.D: This is sin θ, opposite over hypotenuse.

context: What is the value of sin⁻¹(1/2), in degrees?

why.A: This is cos⁻¹(1/2). The cosine of 60°, not the sine, is 1/2.
why.B: Correct — sin⁻¹(1/2) is the angle between −90° and 90° whose sine is 1/2, which is 30°.
why.C: sin 150° is also 1/2, but sin⁻¹ returns only angles from −90° to 90°.
why.D: This reads sin⁻¹ as 1/sin, taking the reciprocal of 1/2. The −1 marks an inverse function, not an exponent.

context: A triangle has an area of 24 square units. Two of its sides measure 8 units and x units, and the angle between them measures 150°. What is the value of x?

why.A: This leaves out the 1/2 at the front of the area formula, solving 4x = 24.
why.B: This uses √3/2 for sin 150°. That is the size of cos 150°; sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2.
why.C: Correct — the area is (1/2)(8)(x) sin 150° = (1/2)(8)(x)(1/2) = 2x, and 2x = 24 gives x = 12.
why.D: This divides the area by the known side, 24 ÷ 8, ignoring the rest of the formula.

context: For 0 ≤ x < 2π, at what value of x does y = 2 sin(x − π/3) + 1 first reach its maximum?

why.A: This is where sin x peaks. The graph is shifted π/3 to the right.
why.B: This shifts the peak π/3 to the left, subtracting instead of adding.
why.C: This is the maximum value of y, 2 + 1, not the x-value where it occurs.
why.D: Correct — sine peaks when its input is π/2, so x − π/3 = π/2 and x = π/2 + π/3 = 5π/6.

context: What are all the solutions of tan x = √3 for 0° ≤ x < 360°?

why.A: Correct — tan 60° = √3, and tangent repeats every 180°, so 60° + 180° = 240° is the other solution.
why.B: This stops at the reference angle. Tangent is also positive in quadrant III.
why.C: This uses the sine pattern, x and 180° − x. At 120° the tangent is −√3.
why.D: These are where tan x = 1/√3. The angle with tangent √3 is 60°.

context: For sin θ ≠ 0 and cos θ ≠ 0, which expression is equal to (1 − cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ)?

why.A: This flips the final fraction. After canceling one sin θ, sin θ is left on top.
why.B: Correct — 1 − cos²θ = sin²θ, and sin²θ/(sin θ cos θ) = sin θ/cos θ = tan θ.
why.C: This cancels the sin θ in the denominator but forgets to divide by cos θ.
why.D: This cancels all of sin²θ against the single sin θ below it.

context: If sin θ + cos θ = 1.2, what is the value of sin θ cos θ?

why.A: This finds 2 sin θ cos θ and forgets to divide by 2.
why.B: This assumes sin θ = cos θ = 0.6. Their sum is 1.2, but 0.6² + 0.6² ≠ 1.
why.C: Correct — squaring gives sin²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ + cos²θ = 1.44. Since sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 2 sin θ cos θ = 0.44.
why.D: This subtracts 1 from 1.2 without squaring first.

context: If sin θ = 1/3, what is the value of cos 2θ?

why.A: This uses 2 sin²θ − 1, which has the sign reversed.
why.B: This doubles sin θ, treating cos 2θ as if it were 2 sin θ.
why.C: This is cos²θ, 1 − sin²θ, which is only one part of cos²θ − sin²θ.
why.D: Correct — cos 2θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ = 1 − 2(1/9) = 7/9.

context: The depth of water at a dock rises and falls between 3 meters and 11 meters. High tide is at t = 0, and the pattern repeats every 12 hours. Which function gives the depth d, in meters, t hours after high tide?

why.A: Correct — the midline is (11 + 3)/2 = 7, the amplitude is (11 − 3)/2 = 4, the period 12 gives 2π/12 = π/6, and cosine starts at its maximum.
why.B: This uses the whole range, 11 − 3, as the amplitude. The amplitude is half of it.
why.C: Sine starts at the midline, so this gives 7 meters at t = 0 instead of high tide.
why.D: This puts the period itself inside the cosine. The coefficient is 2π divided by the period.

context: In triangle ABC, side a = 12 is opposite angle A = 45°, and side b = 8 is opposite angle B. To the nearest tenth of a degree, what is the measure of angle B?

why.A: This angle has the same sine, but with A = 45° the angles would add to more than 180°.
why.B: Correct — the law of sines gives sin B = 8 sin 45°/12 ≈ 0.471, so B ≈ 28.1°. The other angle with that sine, 151.9°, would make A + B more than 180°.
why.C: This uses sin B = 8/12, leaving out sin 45°.
why.D: This swaps the sides, getting sin B = 12 sin 45°/8 ≈ 1.06. With the sides placed correctly the sine is less than 1.

context: Which of the following points lies on the graph of y = log₃ x?

why.A: This swaps the coordinates. It lies on y = 3ˣ, the inverse function.
why.B: log₃ 3 = 1, not 0. The graph crosses the x-axis at (1, 0).
why.C: Correct — log₃ 9 = 2 because 3² = 9.
why.D: This is the y-intercept of y = 3ˣ. A logarithm is not defined at x = 0.

context: If 10ˣ = 0.01, what is the value of x?

why.A: This drops the sign. 10² is 100, not 1/100.
why.B: This counts only the one zero after the decimal point. The 1 is in the hundredths place.
why.C: This is 10ˣ itself, the value 0.01, not the exponent.

context: What is the smallest integer n for which 2ⁿ > 1,000?

why.A: Correct — n > log₂ 1,000 ≈ 9.97, and 2¹⁰ = 1,024 is the first power past 1,000.
why.B: This is too small: 2⁹ = 512.
why.C: This divides 1,000 by 2 instead of asking how many times 2 must be multiplied.
why.D: This is log₁₀ 1,000, which counts powers of 10, not powers of 2.

context: If f(x) = log₂(x − 1), what is the value of f⁻¹(3)?

why.A: This finds x − 1 = 8 and forgets to add the 1 back.
why.B: Correct — f⁻¹(3) is the x with log₂(x − 1) = 3, so x − 1 = 2³ = 8 and x = 9.
why.C: This subtracts 1 from 8 instead of adding it.
why.D: This evaluates f(3) = log₂ 2 = 1, the function rather than its inverse.

context: What is the domain of f(x) = log(5 − 2x)?

why.A: This forgets to reverse the inequality when dividing by −2.
why.B: This allows 5 − 2x = 0, but log 0 is undefined.
why.C: Correct — a logarithm needs a positive input, so 5 − 2x > 0 and x < 5/2.
why.D: This forgets to divide by the 2 in front of x.

context: If ln x = 2 ln 3 − ln 2, what is the value of x?

why.A: This treats the logarithms as plain numbers, computing 2 × 3 − 2.
why.B: This subtracts 9 − 2 instead of dividing. A difference of logarithms is the logarithm of a quotient.
why.C: This ignores the coefficient 2 on ln 3, finding ln 3 − ln 2 = ln(3/2).
why.D: Correct — 2 ln 3 = ln 9, and ln 9 − ln 2 = ln(9/2), so x = 9/2.

context: A car worth $20,000 loses 15% of its value each year, so its value after t years is 20,000(0.85)ᵗ dollars. To the nearest tenth of a year, when is it worth $10,000?

why.A: Correct — 0.85ᵗ = 0.5, so t = log 0.5/log 0.85 ≈ 4.3.
why.B: This takes off 15% of the original $20,000, or $3,000, every year. The loss shrinks as the value drops.
why.C: This uses log 2/log 1.15, treating a 15% loss as undoing a 15% gain. They are not the same.
why.D: This divides the logarithms the wrong way, log 0.85/log 0.5.

context: What are all the solutions of 3²ˣ − 4 · 3ˣ + 3 = 0?

why.A: These are the values of u = 3ˣ. Each still has to be turned into x.
why.B: Correct — with u = 3ˣ, u² − 4u + 3 = 0, so u = 1 or u = 3. Then 3ˣ = 1 gives x = 0, and 3ˣ = 3 gives x = 1.
why.C: This keeps u = 3 but drops u = 1, which gives x = 0 because 3⁰ = 1.
why.D: This flips the signs of the factors, then stops at u.

context: What value or values of x satisfy log₂ x = log₄(x + 12)?

why.A: This keeps x = −3, but a logarithm of a negative number is undefined.
why.B: This keeps the rejected root and drops the valid one.
why.C: Correct — log₄(x + 12) = (1/2) log₂(x + 12), so 2 log₂ x = log₂(x + 12) and x² = x + 12. That gives x = 4 or x = −3, and log₂(−3) is undefined.
why.D: This sets x = x + 12, treating the two bases as if they matched.

context: Using log 2 ≈ 0.301, where log is the base-10 logarithm, how many digits does 2⁵⁰ have?

why.A: This takes 15.05 as the digit count. 10¹⁵ itself already has 16 digits.
why.B: This counts the exponent as the number of digits.
why.C: This halves 50, as if every two factors of 2 added one digit.
why.D: Correct — log 2⁵⁰ = 50 × 0.301 = 15.05, so 2⁵⁰ is between 10¹⁵ and 10¹⁶, and a number of that size has 16 digits.

context: Money in an account grows continuously at 5% a year, so the balance is Pe^(0.05t) after t years. To the nearest tenth of a year, how long does the balance take to triple?

why.B: This divides 3 by 0.05 without taking the natural logarithm of 3.
why.C: This uses ln 2, the time to double, not to triple.
why.D: This uses ln 3/ln 1.05, the tripling time for interest added once a year.
